title: Intracellular Bacterial Imprinting Enables Preservable Whole‐Cell Vaccination
content:
Controlled internalization of attenuated Salmonella establishes a bacterial imprint in whole tumor cells with enhanced immunogenic features. Freeze‐drying preserves key molecular and functional features of this imprint while suppressing proliferative capacity. The resulting FD‐BiT vaccine coordinates antigen‐presenting‐cell activation, T–B‐cell immunity, and memory, establishing bacterial imprinting and imprint preservation as a vaccine‐engineering strategy against primary and metastatic tumors.









ABSTRACT
Whole‐tumor‐cell vaccines preserve broad tumor‐antigen repertoires, but converting living tumor cells into safe and intrinsically immunogenic vaccine substrates remains challenging. Here we generated bacteria‐imprinted tumor (BiT) cells through the controlled internalization of attenuated Salmonella and subsequently prepared them as nonproliferative cellular vaccines by freeze‐drying. Within a defined bacterial‐loading window, intracellular Salmonella induced endoplasmic reticulum stress‐associated immunogenic preprogramming while preserving tumor‐cell integrity, thereby enhancing danger‐signal exposure, antigen‐presentation capacity, and immune visibility. Freeze‐drying preserved the bacteria‐induced immunogenic imprint by retaining key molecular and functional attributes while maintaining overall cellular architecture and markedly reducing residual bacterial viability. Vaccination with freeze‐dried BiT (FD‐BiT) cells elicited coordinated innate and adaptive immune responses, including antigen‐presenting cell activation, T follicular helper‐B‐cell cooperation, and germinal‐center formation. This coordinated T–B cell response was accompanied by durable memory formation and enhanced intratumoral CD8+ T‐cell infiltration, proliferation, and functional maintenance. Accordingly, FD‐BiT reduced primary tumor establishment and pulmonary metastasis and restrained the growth of tumors that emerged despite prophylactic vaccination. These findings establish intracellular bacterial programming and freeze‐drying‐mediated imprint preservation as a cell‐engineering principle for whole‐tumor‐cell vaccination.

title: Engineering Tunable Helper Lipid Architecture to Improve Messenger RNA Lipid Nanoparticle Performance
content:
A library of rationally engineered helper lipids was developed to establish structure‐function relationships governing mRNA‐LNP performance. Integrating molecular simulations, biophysical characterization, and in vivo studies revealed that helper lipid architecture controls membrane fusion, endosomal escape, and delivery efficiency, enabling improved therapeutic and vaccine responses and providing design principles for next‐generation RNA medicines.








ABSTRACT
Helper lipids are essential structural components of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), yet systematic design principles linking helper lipid architecture to messenger RNA (mRNA) delivery performance remain poorly defined. Here we identify helper lipid architecture as a major, largely unexplored design lever for optimizing LNP performance. Using a modular library of more than 80 rationally designed helper lipids, we show that systematic variation in headgroup chemistry, linker topology, and tail cardinality reshapes both LNP biophysical behavior and biological performance. Martini molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with multimodal structural analyses reveal that high‐performing scaffolds undergo a pH‐dependent transition into fusogenic inverse hexagonal‐like ordering, substantially lowering the energetic barrier for endosomal escape. These performance gains persist across the clinically relevant ALC‐0315 and DLin‐MC3‐DMA platforms, establishing helper lipid architecture as a transferable design parameter across distinct ionizable lipid chemistries. Translating these design principles into function, optimized helper lipid formulations restore hepatic protein expression in a mouse model of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency and increase antigen expression and immunogenicity in both preclinical models and in the in vitro human MIMIC platform. Together, these findings establish helper lipids as tunable molecular actuators of potency, tolerability, and stability, offering an engineering framework for next‐generation mRNA vaccines and therapeutics.

title: Advancements in Multi‐Dimensional Hexagonal Boron Nitride‐Based Thermal Management Materials: A Review
content:
Breaking the single dimension heat conduction bottleneck, this review explores the multi‐dimensional synergy of hexagonal boron nitride (BN) in advanced thermal management. By systematically evaluating phonon transport and interfacial thermal resistance across 0D, 1D, and 2D BN, it reveals how multi‐component networks bridge thermal gaps. These insights have guided the design of advanced thermal management materials (TMMs).








ABSTRACT
Hexagonal boron nitride (BN), due to its high thermal conductivity (TC), excellent electrical insulation, and low dielectric constant, has become an ideal filler for designing advanced thermal management materials (TMMs), effectively addressing thermal failure and electromagnetic leakage issues in advanced chips. BN structures in different dimensions (0D, 1D, and 2D) each have their own advantages, their interface morphology directly affects the TC of composite systems. However, there is still a lack of systematic understanding of phonon transport behavior at different interfaces in composite systems and their impact on thermal conduction network construction. This review focuses on dimensional classification and compares the intrinsic TC, phonon transport mechanisms, and network formation behavior of 0D, 1D, and 2D BN fillers. In addition to the traditional filler/polymer interfaces, this analysis also focused on the phonon transport properties at the homogeneous and heterogeneous nanoadditives interfaces of BN. At the same time, the TC of mono‐, di‐, and multi‐component nanoadditives systems were systematically evaluated, revealing the synergistic effects among BN of different dimensions. This review aims to provide a reference for reducing the thermal resistance of complex interfaces and promoting the practical application of micro–nano materials in the field of thermal management.

title: Luminescent and Stable Eu(III) Complex Nanocrystals: A Class of Eu(III) Emitters Toward Amine/Ammonia
content:
Aliphatic‐amine‐based Eu(III) complex nanocrystals are a class of red emissive Eu(III) emitters that show high resistance to emission quenching from environmental amines and exhibit substantially enhanced emission. Pronounced luminescence efficiencies of 51%–64% are obtained from the tri‐n‐decylamine‐based nanocrystals, which are highly stable to amine/ammonia atmosphere and show potential application as UV‐readable red emitters to warning label of amines and ammonia.








ABSTRACT
Eu(III) complexes exhibit highly efficient luminescence, while their emissions are significantly sensitive to amine/ammonia‐induced quenching. Herein, we report a class of Eu(III) complex nanocrystals in which aliphatic amines serve as structural regulators to construct highly luminescent and stable ultrasmall Eu(III) emitters. The addition of aliphatic amines enables the originally insoluble complexes to be dissolved in n‐hexane, producing Eu(III) complex nanocrystal solutions. The primary‐ and secondary‐amine based Eu(btfa)3PBI nanocrystal solutions showed photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs) reaching 24%–36% and 30%–37%, respectively. In a sharp contrast, the complex's luminescence was completely or substantially quenched when dissolved directly in primary or secondary amine liquids, with PLQYs decreasing to 0 or 0.0%–1.2%. The significantly suppressed quenching upon nanocrystal formation originated from the substantial reduction of vibrationally induced nonradiative decays, which was further supported by the low quenching constants toward amines. The nanocrystal's emission was further enhanced upon using the tertiary amines. A remarkable PLQY of 64% was obtained for tri‐n‐decylamine based Eu(dbm)3dmbipy nanocrystals. The nanocrystal solutions exhibited excellent stability, with their PLQYs well retained after 10 h of ambient storage or continuous irradiation with 365 nm UV light. Furthermore, proof‐of‐concept experiments demonstrated the potential application of nanocrystal solids as amine/ammonia‐resistant warning labels.

title: Ultra‐Strong, Leak‐Proof Bio‐Based Polyurethane Ionic Fibers for Sustainable Smart Wearables
content:
Bio‐based polyurethane ionic fibers integrate covalently incorporated ionic liquid units with Mg2+–carbonyl coordination, combining high strength, toughness, and conductivity with low magnesium release. Hydrogen bonding and coordination regulate the polymer network. Woven into smart textiles and coupled with a deep learning framework, these fibers enable full‐body motion monitoring and accurate movement recognition for intelligent wearable applications.








ABSTRACT
Artificial intelligence (AI)‐integrated digital flexible devices have been widely used in motion detection. However, the emphasis on sensitivity and response speed often overlooks environmental sustainability. Based on a green‐mechanical‐electrical synergistic design, a polar coordination and chemical confinement strategy is proposed to fabricate an ion‐conductive polyurethane fiber. Specifically, chemical confinement refers to the covalent incorporation of the polymerizable ionic‐liquid component into the polyurethane backbone through its hydroxyl‐functionalized imidazolium moiety. Polar coordination involves reversible Mg2+–carbonyl interactions that contribute to mechanical reinforcement and Mg2+ retention. The resulting fiber exhibits a tensile strength of 52.75 MPa and an elongation at break of 1414%. Meanwhile, the in situ grafted ionic liquid provides an ionic conductivity of 0.209 mS cm−1. After 120 h of vigorous stirring in water, the Mg concentration in the test medium reached 1.9 ppm, showing limited Mg release under the tested condition. Integrating this fiber into smart fabrics enables full‐body motion monitoring and accurate recognition of complex movements with 100% accuracy. This study establishes a closed‐loop paradigm from sustainable molecular design to AI‐driven decision‐making, offering new material design insights for next‐generation green, safe, and high‐performance smart wearable devices.

title: An Implantable In‐Tube System for Quantitative Precision Vagus Neuromodulation and Feedback of Intestinal Motility
content:
An implantable closed‐loop system with an ionic piezoelectric sensor, chip, electrode, and display enables precision vagus neuromodulation and real‐time motility feedback. Its radial‐gradient hydrogel and stress‐concentration design quantify intensity, frequency, duration, and local compression rate. In‐situ feedback optimizes stimulation to a 5–10 Hz window, providing a self‐driven bioelectronic solution for brain–gut axis studies and intestinal disease intervention.








ABSTRACT
Electrical vagus neuromodulation of intestinal motility has demonstrated significant clinical utility in the field, where targeting the brain–gut axis can serve as an adjunct in treating intestinal diseases. However, quantitatively understanding vagus‐intestine interoceptive information about real‐time and in situ feedback on intestinal motility under the influence of electrical stimulation parameters is one of the most urgent challenges. Here we propose an implantable closed‐loop system that combines a scalable catheter‐type ionic piezoelectric (in‐tube) sensor as diverse as the gut, a microelectronic chip, an electrical vagus stimulation electrode, and a display interface to realize point‐of‐care precision vagus neuromodulation and feedback of intestinal motility. Owing to the radial gradient hydrogel structure design and stress concentration effect, the in‐tube sensor can simultaneously quantitatively detect and display four key parameters of intestinal motility, including intensity, frequency, duration, and local compression rate, with a high sensitivity of 7.0 mV mmHg−1 and unique pressure–time integral behavior with a time sensitivity of 24.1 mV s−1, making up for the deficiency of traditional sensors that cannot obtain pressure duration. After implanting the in‐tube sensor in the anatomically challenging intestinal lumen of rabbits, we intuitively show how electrical vagus stimulation affects intestinal motility, which guides the optimal frequency window of 5 ∼ 10 Hz.

title: π‑Conjugated Helical Polymer for Circularly Polarized Photodetection and Secure Optoelectronic Encoding
content:
By directly inducing helical structure into the diPDI backbone, helical polymer (SSSS)‐diPDI‐C8‐T‐T was successfully constructed, enabling record‐high |gph| of 1.03 among reported single‐component chiral polymers, as well as dual‐wavelength CPL‐PUF (λ = 405 and 535 nm) with enhanced security and unpredictability for optical encryption.








ABSTRACT
Helical polymers are promising materials for circularly polarized light (CPL) detection and hardware‐level information security owing to their tunable chiroptical properties, efficient charge transport, and intrinsic conformational randomness. However, designing helical polymers with high chiroptical activity, which can be effectively translated intohigh‐performance CPL detection remains challenging. Herein, we reported the helical polymer, (SSSS)‐diPDI‐C8‐T‐T, in which point chirality was effectively transferred to π‐extended diperylene diimide (diPDI) backbone. Compared with non‐helical polymer (SS)‐PDI‐C8‐T‐T, (SSSS)‐diPDI‐C8‐T‐T exhibited chiroptical activity (the absorption dissymmetry factors, gabs = −1.4 × 10−3 at 460 nm) in chloroform (10−5 M), owing to the optimized electric–magnetic (µ‐m) transition dipole alignment. CPL detectors based on (SSSS)‐diPDI‐C8‐T‐T annealed thin films exhibited higher average photocurrent dissymmetry factors (gph) of 0.52 at 535 nm and −1.03 at 405 nm, the latter of which is the highest gph reported for single‐component chiral polymer‐based CPL detection. The enhanced chirality‐induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect increased the spin polarization to 89.03%, contributing to the higher gph for (SSSS)‐diPDI‐C8‐T‐T annealed thin films. Leveraging the dual‐wavelength CPL response of (SSSS)‐diPDI‐C8‐T‐T annealed thin films and spatial randomness, 5 × 8 CPL‐PUF array enabled optoelectronic fingerprinting, with inter‐ and intra‐Hamming distances of 49.278% and 1.655%, respectively. This work highlights helical polymers for CPL detection and chiral optoelectronic fingerprinting.

title: Orthogonal Self‐Assembled Two‐Dimensional Charge‐Transfer Cocrystals With Superior Photothermal Stability for Low‐Loss NIR‐II Waveguiding and Epitaxial Heterostructure Fabrication
content:
The donor DTBDT with an extended π‐conjugated structure was selected to self‐assemble with the acceptor TCNQ into CT cocrystals. The expanded π‐conjugated plane significantly enhances intermolecular orbital hybridization, red‐shifting the emission into the NIR‐II region peaking at 1050 nm. Meanwhile, a interaction network with orthogonal orientations was established into the system to direct 2D crystal growth. It also endows the cocrystal with excellent structural and photothermal stability, as well as multi‐directional optical waveguiding with low‐loss. Furthermore, a branched heterostructure featuring efficient ET and cross‐band optical signal conversion was successfully constructed.








ABSTRACT
Low‐dimensional organic near‐infrared (NIR) crystals hold tremendous potential for integrated photonics. However, simultaneously achieving two‐dimensional (2D) structural growth and low‐loss waveguiding within the NIR‐II region remains a formidable challenge due to one‐dimensional (1D) packing tendencies imposed by strong charge transfer (CT) interactions. In this study, we strategically choose the extended π‐conjugated structure donor dithieno[2,3‐d:2',3'‐d']benzo[1,2‐b:4,5‐b']dithiophene and the strong electron‐withdrawing acceptor tetracyanoquinodimethane, and report the first large‐scale preparation of 2D organic CT cocrystal microsheets with NIR‐II emission at 1050 nm via a gas‐phase self‐assembly. The strategically expanded conjugation framework not only further promotes the luminescence red‐shift but also introduces an interaction network with orthogonal directions, counterbalancing the intrinsic 1D stacking constraints brought by the strong CT interactions and guiding the crystals into a thermodynamically stable 2D morphology. The compact network plays a crucial role in endowing the material with exceptional structural and photothermal stability, as well as low‐loss optical waveguiding. Furthermore, attributed to the extremely low lattice‐mismatch rate, 1D‐2D branched heterostructures were constructed, which demonstrated efficient energy transfer (ET) and cross‐band optical signal conversion over 600 nm. This work breaks new ground in extending 2D organic cocrystals into the NIR‐II region and provides a promising material platform for low‐loss, and integrated NIR optoelectronic devices.

title: 3D‐Printable Bioinspired Heterostructured Polymer With Exceptional Toughness and Fatigue Resistance
content:
A bioinspired heterostructure (BIHS) strategy breaking the toughness‐fatigue trade‐off in polymer was proposed. BIHS enables stress redistribution at crack tips and activates multiple energy‐dissipation pathways, thereby effectively suppressing crack propagation. We further develop a BIHS‐IVD that withstands 1.5 × 107 cycles without failure under physiological loading in saline conditions, corresponding to an estimated 45‐year cycle‐equivalent fatigue life.








ABSTRACT
Polymeric materials are widely used in load‐bearing biomedical applications, yet achieving concurrent high fracture toughness and fatigue resistance remains a longstanding challenge due to their intrinsic trade‐off. Here, we propose a bioinspired heterostructure (BIHS) fatigue‐resistant strategy inspired by the material‐structure synergy of natural intervertebral discs (IVDs). The optimized BIHS composite achieves a fracture toughness of 1252 ± 70.13 kJ/m2 and a fatigue threshold of 8010 J/m2, outperforming conventional polymer materials. The BIHS enables stress redistribution at crack tips and activates multiple energy‐dissipation pathways, including crack bridging and deflection, fiber pull‐out and rupture, and interfacial interactions, thereby suppressing crack initiation and propagation under cyclic loading. Leveraging this design, we further develop a BIHS‐IVD that withstands 1.5 × 107 cycles without failure under physiological loading in saline conditions, corresponding to an estimated 45‐year cycle‐equivalent fatigue life. These results establish a generalizable bioinspired design framework for durable polymeric materials and provide a promising pathway toward long‐lasting biomedical implants.

title: Ultrarobust and Thermo‐Mechano‐Photo‐Responsive Elastomers by Supramolecular and Dynamic 3D Topological Architectures
content:
In this work, hierarchically engineered ultrarobust elastomer networks with supramolecular nanodomains via dynamic covalent/supramolecular synergy are successfully constructed. This multifunctional system integrates thermo‐mechano‐photonic responsiveness: (1) Thermally triggered nanophase separation through supramolecular reassembly. (2) Stress‐induced crystallization driving 3D topological evolution for in situ nano‐reinforcement. (3) Temperature‐mediated photo‐responsive reconfiguration enabling photolithographic encryption and patterning.








ABSTRACT
Mechanically robust elastomers are being widely used in multi‐stimuli‐responsive systems including closed‐loop recycling, information encryption, and advanced photolithography. However, their advancement is hindered by an inherent trade‐off: structural integrity for mechanical robustness versus molecular‐level reversibility for stimuli responsiveness. In this study, we constructed ultrarobust recyclable and photo‐responsive supramolecular‐dynamic covalent networks (SDCN) based on molecular engineering of anthracene‐functionalized poly(urethane‐urea‐amide) (PUUA) networks with hindered urea motifs. Well‐designed SDCN achieves multiscale assembly through coordinated π–π stacking, hydrogen bonding, and dynamic covalent interactions, creating dynamic coupling between soft‐chain crosslinks and self‐assembly hard domains, and driving microphase separation. Under stretching, strain‐activated disassembly of dynamically assembled nanostructures synergizes with stress‐induced crystallization, in situ evolving three‐dimensional topological architectures and promoting strength‐toughness enhancement. Consequently, PUUA elastomers exhibit remarkable mechanical performance (100.17 MPa tensile strength, 1286.79% elongation and 498.15 MJ m−3 toughness at room temperature; 113.67 MPa strength and 667.8% elongation at −40°C) and recycling performance (92.4% recyclability via solvent reprocessing). Significantly, UV‐responsive anthracene photonic moieties combined with temperature‐mediated interfacial SDCN transition enable fluorescent encryption and sub‐micron photolithographic patterning. Therefore, this work coordinates dynamic thermal‐mechanical‐optical responses and multi‐scale molecular transition mechanisms, which can be expected to boost high‐precision photolithographic patterning and flexible microcircuit printing fields.

title: Halide Perovskite Heterojunction Crossbar Arrays for Selector‐Free Analog In‐Memory Computing
content:
Passive memristor crossbar arrays require selectors to suppress sneak currents, complicating integration. A discrete 3D/2D halide perovskite heterojunction, formed in situ, endows each symmetric cell with intrinsic rectification and analog memory. A selector‐free 32 × 32 array with 1024 individually measured cells (99.4% yield) supports analog image programming and measurement‐constrained inference, offering a low‐temperature route to in‐memory computing.








ABSTRACT
Passive memristor crossbars require each cell to suppress sneak‐path currents while retaining gradual, reproducible conductance programmability. In halide perovskites, however, sneak‐current suppression and analog programmability have rarely been integrated and validated across passive arrays. Fabricated arrays have typically relied on peripheral circuitry to mitigate parasitic currents, whereas self‐rectifying analog memristors have largely remained at the single‐device level. Here, a discrete three‐dimensional/two‐dimensional (3D/2D) FAPbI3/BDAPbI4 heterojunction, formed through controlled in situ conversion, is shown to integrate diode‐like rectification and analog resistive switching within a single, nominally symmetric Au/perovskite/Au cell. The 3D perovskite enables field‐assisted ion migration, while the 2D perovskite introduces an interfacial barrier that induces asymmetric transport, resulting in intrinsic rectification and stable analog switching. A 32 × 32 passive crossbar array comprising 1024 cells, fabricated on silicon below 150°C, exhibits a 99.4% functional‐device yield, a synaptic nonlinearity of 0.007, and stable operation over 640 000 programming pulses. Cell‐resolved measurements demonstrate analog image programming and erasing, and a tiled‐array inference model incorporating the measured cell characteristics and electrical nonidealities connects the experimentally realized array to in‐memory‐computing performance. These results establish chemically defined perovskite heterojunctions as a low‐temperature, silicon‐compatible materials strategy for selector‐free analog in‐memory computing.

title: Topological‐Insulator‐Based Ion‐Electron‐Coupled Nanochannels With a Photothermally Induced Thermoelectric Field for Enhanced Ionic Transport
content:
Layered Bi2Te3/MXene nanochannels synergistically enhance ion transport through highly polar interfaces, rapid interfacial electronic responses, and photothermally induced thermoelectric fields. Ion–electron coupling reduces the ion‐migration activation energy by 34.6%, enabling an osmotic power density of 18.9 W m−2 under a 50‐fold NaCl gradient, further increasing to 25.5 W m−2 upon illumination.








ABSTRACT
Efficient ion transport is essential for high‐performance energy storage and conversion, yet strong ion–channel interactions in conventional highly polar nanochannels can increase migration barriers and impede rapid ion motion. Here, we report layered ion‐electron‐coupled Bi2Te3/Ti3C2Tx nanochannels, in which ion transport is synergistically regulated by highly polar interfaces, highly conductive surface states, and a photothermally induced thermoelectric field. The polar MXene interfaces support selective ion transport, whereas the highly conductive surface states of Bi2Te3 enhance interfacial electronic responsiveness, facilitating charge equilibration and mitigating local charge accumulation during ion migration. This interfacial coupling reduces the ion‐transport activation energy to 8.02 kJ mol−1, 34.6% lower than that of pristine MXene nanochannels. As a functional demonstration of enhanced ion transport, the nanochannels deliver a 5.56‐fold increase in osmotic power density (18.9 W m−2) under a 50‐fold NaCl concentration gradient. Upon illumination, the photothermally induced temperature gradient activates the Seebeck response of Bi2Te3, providing an additional thermoelectric driving force for directional ion migration, as reflected by a further increase in power density to 25.5 W m−2. This work provides a strategy for enhancing ion transport under nanoconfinement through interfacial‐electronic‐coupling‐mediated regulation and thermoelectric‐field‐assisted driving.

title: Spatiotemporally Controlled Lithium Delivery via a Graphene‐Hydrogel System for Wnt Activation and Spinal Cord Repair
content:
To activate pro‐regenerative Wnt for treating spinal cord injury (SCI), a novel graphene lithium hydrogel (GLH)‐based approach is developed. GLH controllably releases Li+ and scavenges ROS via graphene‐stabilized lithium. Li+ activates Wnt in both iPSC‐based models and a murine SCI model. Wnt synergizes with ROS scavenging for reducing scar formation and enhancing neural regeneration with robust functional recovery after SCI.








ABSTRACT
Wnt signaling plays essential roles in neural development and has significant potential to promote regeneration after central nervous system (CNS) injury. However, therapeutic strategies that locally modulate Wnt signaling in vivo remain limited. Herein, we develop a battery‐inspired graphene‐lithium hydrogel (GLH) that enables sustained, controllable delivery of lithium ions (Li+) to injury sites. Li+ inhibits glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β), activating pro‐regenerative Wnt/β‐catenin signaling. Beyond Wnt activation, GLH provides complementary therapeutic functions: oxidation of lithium (0) attenuates reactive oxygen species‐associated stress, while the gelatin‐based hydrogel matrix supplies a permissive extracellular matrix (ECM)‐like niche. In co‐cultures of human‐induced pluripotent stem cell‐derived neural progenitor cells and macrophages, GLH suppresses pro‐inflammatory signaling and enhances neurogenesis. In a murine spinal cord injury complete transection model, a single GLH injection sustains Wnt activation for over one week, reduces acute neuroinflammation and astroglial/fibrotic scarring, and promotes long‐term tissue preservation and functional recovery. Transcriptomic and protein analyses further support coordinated modulation of Wnt‐related, redox, inflammatory, and ECM‐remodeling pathways, accompanying improved locomotor and bladder function and reduced neuropathic pain. Given the conserved role of Wnt signaling in regeneration, the GLH offers a multifunctional materials platform with potential applicability beyond the CNS.

title: Interfacial Electronic Reconstruction Activates TiO2 in MnO2/TiO2 Heterostructures for Accelerated Sulfur Redox Chemistry
content:
A chemically integrated MnO2/TiO2 heterointerface containing residual carbon induces interfacial electronic reconstruction, modulating Ti‐derived states and enhancing their responsiveness toward polysulfides. This reconstructed interface strengthens sulfur‐intermediate interactions, accelerates bidirectional sulfur redox conversion, and enables durable lithium–sulfur batteries, with DFT providing microscopic mechanistic insight into charge redistribution.








ABSTRACT
Lithium–sulfur batteries are promising for next‐generation energy storage but are limited by sluggish sulfur redox kinetics originating from insufficient regulation of interfacial electronic structures. Here, we report a MnO2/TiO2 heterostructure with integrated interfacial bonding, in which residual carbon is inherently incorporated into the interfacial region. The characterizations reveal pronounced reconstruction of the local coordination and electronic environment upon heterostructure formation, including Ti─O─Mn bonding, reduced Ti states, and substantial changes in the surface potential and valence‐band structure. DFT calculations suggest that the reconstructed interface involves the coexistence of net intercomponent charge redistribution and localized bond polarization, with residual carbon contributing to interfacial electronic coupling. Consistent with this reconstructed electronic environment, Ti‐derived sites exhibit enhanced electronic response toward polysulfides, while MnO2 and residual carbon contribute to the coupled interfacial structure. Consequently, MnO2/TiO2 catalyst enables stable cycling under a high sulfur loading of 9.2 mg cm−2 and, when integrated as a functional interlayer, allows the sulfur cathode to deliver a high specific capacity of 1569 mAh g−1 together with durability over 1000 cycles, with a capacity decay rate of 0.054% per cycle. This work highlights chemically integrated oxide heterointerfaces as an effective platform for regulating local electronic structures and accelerating sulfur redox chemistry.

title: Reconceptualizing Thermal Runaway Mechanisms in Sulfide Solid‐State Batteries via Dynamic Interfacial Reconstruction
content:
Challenging the perceived “intrinsic safety” of sulfide solid‐state batteries, this Perspective identifies dynamic interfacial reconstruction during cycling as the decisive trigger for thermal runaway. The resulting metastable interphases act as thermochemical igniters that lower onset barriers and drive staged exothermic cascades, providing a new interface‐centric paradigm for designing resilient solid‐state energy systems.








ABSTRACT
The commercialization of sulfide‐based all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) is often predicated on their perceived “intrinsic safety”. However, recent evidence of violent thermal runaway under abuse conditions has shattered this consensus, revealing a sobering gap in our mechanistic understanding of solid‐state failure. In this Perspective, we argue that the current stagnation in safety research stems from a “liquid‐legacy” mindset that fails to account for the unique solid–solid reactive landscape. We propose that the thermal failure of sulfide ASSBs is fundamentally governed by a dynamic interfacial reconstruction involving the continuous electrochemical and chemo‐mechanical evolution of the interphase during cycling. By deconstructing the staged thermochemical cascade, we demonstrate how cycling‐induced metastable species, such as polysulfides and mixed‐conducting interphases, act as reactive “pre‐conditioners” that dictate failure pathways. This framework explains long‐standing experimental inconsistencies, including divergent SO2 evolution profiles and fluctuating trigger temperatures across identical material couples. This shift from a static material‐centric view to a dynamic interface‐centric framework reframes the rational design of truly robust, next‐generation energy storage systems.

title: Flexible 2D Donor‐Acceptor MOFs Enable Tunable and Pressure‐Responsive TSCT–TADF for Heterocrystal Photonic Logic
content:
The regulation of solid‐state TSCT–TADF materials remains changing. Leveraging flexible 2D D–A MOFs as a versatile platform, we achieve highly tunable and optimized TADF emission through synergistic integration of solvent‐directed D–A stacking control, ligand engineering, and high‐pressure engineering, and further construct D–A MOF heterocrystals that enable optical logic gate operations under high pressure.








ABSTRACT
Efficient thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) materials that combine high efficiency, color tunability, and dynamic stimulus responsiveness are highly desirable for adaptive photonic technologies, yet remain difficult to realize within a single crystalline platform. Here, flexible two‐dimensional (2D) donor‐acceptor (D–A) metal‐organic frameworks (MOFs) are developed through integrating an aggregation‐induced‐emission‐active triphenylamine donor with size‐matched electron‐deficient acceptors. Solvent‐directed assembly, donor conformational flexibility, and acceptor electronic modulation cooperatively regulate the D–A packing and through‐space charge‐transfer (TSCT) effect. The resulting MOFs exhibit broadly tunable TADF emission (474–635 nm), delayed lifetimes (0.11–7.65 µs), and photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY, 0.52%–74.24%). Relative to the DMF‐derived structures, the DMA‐derived MOFs display increases of up to 51‐fold in delayed lifetime and 6‐fold in PLQY, while calculations support an unconventional high‐lying reverse intersystem crossing (hRISC) pathway. More importantly, the structural adaptability of the layered frameworks enables pressure‐induced reconfiguration of D–A interactions, giving rise to reversible piezochromic TSCT–TADF with emission shifts of up to 113 nm. A multicomponent heterocrystal is further constructed to translate pressure‐dependent emission changes into optical logic operations. These results establish flexible 2D D–A MOFs as a dynamic platform for integrating efficient TADF, mechanical responsiveness, and heterocrystal photonic functionality.

title: Sequential Regulation of Dendrite Initiation and Propagation for High‐Current Hydroborate‐Based Solid‐State Sodium Metal Batteries
content:
A dual‐interlayer strategy sequentially regulates sodium dendrite initiation and propagation in hydroborate‐based all‐solid‐state batteries. A Sn/C interlayer promotes uniform sodium deposition, while an internal sulfide interlayer blocks dendrite propagation through localized reactions. This complementary regulation enables stable cycling at high current densities and improves full‐cell performance, providing a practical approach to stabilizing solid‐state sodium metal batteries.








ABSTRACT
Hydroborate solid electrolytes (SEs) offer fast Na+ transport, low density, and compatibility with Na metal, yet their current tolerance is restricted by dendrite‐induced short circuits in all‐solid‐state Na metal batteries (ASSNBs). Here, a spatially coordinated dual‐interlayer architecture is developed to regulate dendrite initiation and propagation in Na4B10H10B12H12 (NBH)‐based ASSNBs. At the Na|NBH interface, a three‐dimensional Sn/C framework enables Na infiltration into the porous scaffold and homogenizes current distribution, while dynamically formed Na–Sn sites facilitate Na+ transport and redistribution, thereby maintaining intimate interfacial contact and suppressing dendrite initiation. Within the NBH SE, a Na2.9375PS3.9375Cl0.0625 (NPSC) sulfide interlayer reacts with penetrating Na to suppress dendrite propagation, with crack‐like pathways terminating near the NBH|NPSC interface. This sequential regulation increases the critical current density from 0.5 to 3.3 mA cm−2. Symmetric cells operate stably for 7000 and 1000 h at 0.5 and 3.0 mA cm−2, respectively. Full cells with an O3‐type NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 cathode retain 75% capacity after 800 cycles at 2 C, while supporting cathode loadings up to 15 mg cm−2. This work establishes sequential control of dendrite initiation and propagation as a design principle for high‐current hydroborate‐based ASSNBs.

title: High‐Density Colossal Barocaloric Effect in Quasi‐Spherical Ionic Plastic Crystal (Et4N)(CrO3Cl)
content:
In this work, we explored an ionic plastic crystal that demonstrates high‐density barocaloric refrigeration capabilities in multiple dimensions. After analysis, the high‐density barocaloric effect of it mainly stems from its quasi‐spherical structure, relatively weak hydrogen bonds, and significant volume change. Furthermore, this work has broken the limitation that the research on high‐density barocaloric materials was confined to inorganic materials.








ABSTRACT
The barocaloric effect driven by hydrostatic pressure of solid‐state phase transition materials is regarded as one of the means to replace traditional vapor compression refrigeration technology due to its environmental friendliness and high efficiency. However, the refrigeration density of the currently reported solid‐state barocaloric refrigerants is generally low, which is not conducive to the low cost and miniaturization of refrigeration equipment. In order to solve this problem, we explore the barocaloric effect of ionic plastic crystal (Et4N)(CrO3Cl), which shows a high refrigeration density due to weak hydrogen bond interaction, quasi‐spherical structure, and large volume change during the first‐order phase transition. Under a driving pressure of 100 MPa, the reversible isothermal entropy changes (ΔSit, rev) per unit mass and per unit volume are 284.1 J kg−1 K−1 and 0.397 J cm−3 K−1, respectively. Regardless of the evaluation from any perspective, this refrigerant shows a high refrigeration density. In addition, (Et4N)(CrO3Cl) shows relatively high‐pressure sensitivity (dTtdP=0.225KMPa−1$\frac{\mathrm{d}{T}_{\mathrm{t}}}{\mathrm{d}P}=0.225\ \mathrm{K}\mathrm{MP}{\mathrm{a}}^{-1}$dTtdP=0.225K·MPa−1$\frac{{{\mathrm{d}}{{T}_{\mathrm{t}}}}}{{{\mathrm{d}}P}} = 0.225{\mathrm{\ K}}\cdot{\mathrm{MP}}{{{\mathrm{a}}}^{ - 1}}$). This also enables it to exhibit excellent refrigeration capacity (RC = 3636 J kg−1 = 5.08 J cm−3) at a relatively low pressure (100 MPa). The discovery of this high‐density barocaloric refrigerant will help to promote the research on the miniaturization of refrigeration equipment.

title: Synergistic Bimolecular Reconstruction of the Perovskite‐Carbon Interface Enables 23.6%‐Efficiency Fully Printable Mesoscopic Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
Synergistic bimolecular interfacial programming unlocks the hidden potential of hole‐conductor‐free, printable mesoscopic perovskite solar cells. Sequential surface polishing and molecular grafting reconstruct the perovskite‐carbon interface and optimize hole collection, yielding an exceptional 23.6% power conversion efficiency and promising broad prospects for low‐cost, scalable photovoltaics.








ABSTRACT
Hole‐conductor‐free, fully printable mesoscopic perovskite solar cells (p‐MPSCs) hold compelling promise for photovoltaic industrialization. However, their power conversion efficiency (PCE) remains constrained by limited hole collection at the perovskite‐carbon interface. Here, we introduce a synergistic bimolecular post‐treatment using toluene diisocyanate (TDI) and 4‐methyl sulfonyl phenyl methylammonium chloride (MSBH) to reconstruct this critical interface. We demonstrate that TDI reacts with surface formamidinium to polish and activate the perovskite terminations, while MSBH subsequently grafts onto this activated surface. This combined action simultaneously reconstructs the interface with optimized surface energy band bending and minimized interfacial defects, thereby facilitating hole extraction and suppressing non‐radiative recombination. Consequently, this strategy elevates the PCE of small‐area p‐MPSCs (0.1 cm2) to 23.6%. Furthermore, it enables the fabrication of a p‐MPSC minimodule with an active area of 52.7 cm2, achieving a PCE of 22.1%, among the highest values ever reported for carbon‐based, fully printable architectures. Devices retained 98% of their initial PCE after 750 h of operational stability testing at 55°C ± 5°C. This work provides an effective interface reconstruction strategy that concurrently addresses defect passivation and energy alignment, paving the way for high‐performance, stable, and scalable cost‐effective perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Progress in Heterogeneous Nucleation‐Induced Crystallization Strategies in Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
This review comprehensively examines heterogeneous nucleation‐induced crystallization for perovskite photovoltaics, elucidating mechanisms from thermodynamic, lattice‐matching and solution‐chemistry perspectives. It categorizes functional material systems, including perovskite seeds, low‐dimensional templates and organic additives, and highlights their transformative impact on device efficiency, defect suppression, and operational stability across single‐junction and tandem architectures, while charting future research directions.








ABSTRACT
The performance of perovskite solar cells is fundamentally capped by the crystalline quality of perovskite active layers. Conventional solution‐processing lacks kinetic control over nucleation, engendering granular heterogeneity, trap‐state proliferation and halide phase segregation. Heterogeneous nucleation‐induced crystallization circumvents these bottlenecks by deploying extrinsic seeds or templates to engineer nucleation sites and orchestrate crystallization trajectories. This review systematically examines recent advances in this strategy. It begins by explaining the mechanisms from thermodynamic, lattice‐matching and solution‐chemistry perspectives, emphasizing the reduction of nucleation barriers and the guided alignment of crystal orientation. We then categorize the functional material systems, like perovskite seeds, low‐dimensional materials and organic molecules. The discussion extends to the significant performance improvements achieved by this strategy in single‐junction, wide‐bandgap and tandem solar cells, notably in enhanced efficiency, suppressed defects and reinforced stability. Relate mechanisms for stability improvement, like grain boundary reduction, ion migration inhibition and strain release, are also discussed. Finally, we outline prospective research trajectories to provide theoretical frameworks for advancing high‐efficiency and stable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Pulsed Electrocatalysis: A Novel Paradigm of Nitrate Reduction
content:
Pulsed electrolysis makes nitrate reduction from a conventional steady‐state process into a dynamically tunable interfacial reaction. Periodic modulation of the applied potential and/or current restores catalyst activity, enriches interfacial nitrate, regulates key intermediate generation and conversion, and alleviates mass‐transfer limitations. Beyond ammonia synthesis, this strategy opens opportunities for producing value‐added nitrogen‐containing chemicals.








ABSTRACT
Electrocatalytic nitrate (NO3−) reduction reaction (eNO3RR) offers a promising route for NO3− pollution control and nitrogen resource recovery. However, under conventional potentiostatic electrolysis, limited product selectivity and catalyst deactivation still hinder its practical application. Pulsed electrolysis provides a new strategy to dynamically regulate the complex interfacial reaction processes in eNO3RR. Nevertheless, its effectiveness strongly depends on rational parameter design, as inappropriate pulse settings may increase energy consumption and induce undesired catalyst structural evolution. More importantly, the relationship between pulse parameters and interfacial reaction mechanisms remains unclear. Thereby, current parameter optimization lacks generalizable design principles. In this review, we summarize recent advances in pulsed electrolysis for eNO3RR, focusing on its mechanistic roles in dynamic catalyst reconstruction, interfacial microenvironment regulation, and reaction pathway modulation. We then outline design considerations for key pulse parameters and analyze their effects on catalyst stability, mass transport, Faradaic efficiency, and product selectivity. We further discuss the potential of pulsed strategies for value‐added C─N coupling transformations. Finally, we examine the key challenges facing pulsed eNO3RR in energy efficiency, stability, and practical scale‐up. This review aims to provide mechanistic insights and design guidance for pulsed eNO3RR systems and to support their transition from laboratory studies toward sustainable practical applications.

title: Fluorinated Gel Polymer Electrolytes for Lithium Metal Batteries: From Passive Protection to Adaptive Interfacial Regulation
content:
Fluorinated gel polymer electrolytes (FGPEs) enable a transition from passive interfacial protection toward adaptive interfacial regulation in lithium metal batteries. Through synergistic regulation of interfacial chemistry, Li+ transport, and mechanical adaptability, FGPEs accommodate dynamic interfacial evolution induced by repeated Li plating/stripping, enabling stable lithium deposition and durable long‐term cycling.








ABSTRACT
Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) are promising candidates for next‐generation high‐energy‐density energy storage. However, their practical application is hindered by dendritic lithium growth and unstable electrode–electrolyte interfaces. Fluorinated gel polymer electrolytes (FGPEs) have emerged as attractive electrolyte systems because they combine enhanced safety with liquid‐like interfacial contact. Through fluorine‐mediated regulation of Li+ solvation and interfacial chemistry, FGPEs can improve the stability of lithium metal anodes. This review discusses the transition of FGPEs from passive interfacial protection to dynamic interfacial regulation. A unified framework for designing adaptive interfaces is proposed, emphasizing their ability to respond to electrochemical, mechanical, and ion‐transport variations during battery operation. Recent advances in weak intermolecular interactions, molecular interfacial engineering, and functional fillers are summarized with a focus on their roles in regulating solvation structures, interphase chemistry, and Li+ transport. Furthermore, emerging insights from operando characterization, multiscale simulations, and multiphysics modeling are discussed to elucidate the dynamic evolution of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and lithium deposition behavior. By linking molecular interactions with interfacial evolution and electrochemical performance, this review provides design principles for developing advanced FGPEs toward practical high‐energy‐density LMBs.

title: Radiation‐Resilient Perovskite Solar Cells for Space Exploration: From Soft‐Lattice Dynamics to Stack‐Level Hardening
content:
Space radiation deposits energy in perovskite solar cells through NIEL and IEL pathways, generating lattice defects and ionization damage while also enabling soft‐lattice dynamic self‐healing. This review connects radiation energy deposition, device‐level degradation, and stack‐level hardening, highlighting lattice engineering, interface stabilization, and barrier protection as key strategies for radiation‐resilient perovskite‐based space photovoltaics.








ABSTRACT
Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as compelling candidates for next‐generation space photovoltaics, offering high specific power, mechanical flexibility, and promising radiation tolerance. However, in orbit, these devices face a harsh radiation environment of energetic electrons, protons, gamma rays, ultraviolet (UV) photons, and other radiation sources such as neutrons and x‐rays, together with vacuum, AM0 illumination, and temperature cycling. Here, we review radiation damage mechanisms and hardening strategies for PSCs under space‐relevant conditions. We highlight that the soft ionic lattice and defect tolerance of halide perovskites enable dynamic self‐healing capability, wherein non‐ionizing energy loss (NIEL)‐driven displacement damage competes with ionizing energy loss (IEL)‐driven defect reorganization. Despite the perovskite absorber's exceptional radiation hardness, device‐level failure is frequently dictated by the degradation of charge‐transport layers, buried interfaces, metal contacts, substrates, and encapsulation layers. We then discuss hardening strategies, including compositional engineering, robust transport layers, interfacial passivation, and functional encapsulation. Finally, we outline key challenges limiting practical deployment, including the lack of standardized space‐relevant testing protocols, insufficient understanding of multi‐physics coupled space stressors, and the absence of predictive lifetime models. By bridging fundamental radiation physics with device engineering, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing radiation‐resilient perovskite photovoltaics for aerospace applications.

title: On‐Stage and Behind‐the‐Scenes: Solvent‐Directed Structural Transformation and Optical Properties of Metal Clusters
content:
Solvent plays a decisive role in regulating the structural transformation of metal clusters. Variations in solvent environments trigger diverse pathways, including isomerization, size evolution, and assembly conversion. These structural changes are governed by coordination interactions and environmental factors, leading to tunable optical responses such as emission shifts and intensity modulation, highlighting the dynamic interplay between solvent, structure, and properties.








ABSTRACT
Understanding the intrinsic relationship between structure conversion and property response is one of the central challenges in the design of functional materials. In recent years, atomically precise metal clusters, featuring highly tunable geometrical configurations and discrete electronic energy levels, have emerged as ideal model systems for elucidating structure–property correlations. Among various external stimuli that trigger structural transformations of metal clusters, solvents play a unique and active role: beyond serving as reaction or dissolution media, they can systematically induce diverse structural conversions of metal clusters and thereby profoundly modulate their optical properties. In view of the current lack of a unified theoretical framework connecting solvent‐directed structural conversion with optical responses of metal clusters, this review first systematically summarizes the typical types of solvent‐induced structural transformations in metal clusters. It then provides an in‐depth analysis of the microscopic mechanisms underlying solvent‐driven structural evolution and their intrinsic influence on optical properties. Finally, the fundamental issues, remaining challenges, and future perspectives in this emerging field are discussed. This review aims to provide a theoretical foundation and methodological guidance for solvent‐controlled structural transformations and optical performance optimization of metal clusters.

title: Thermo‐Optically Engineered Radiative Cooling Materials With Tailored Thermal Conduction
content:
Radiative cooling performance is governed not only by spectral regulation but also by how heat is conducted, spread, or blocked before reaching the emitting surface. This Review organizes thermo‐optical materials into thermally insulated, highly thermally conductive, and thermal‐rectified strategies, linking heat‐flow requirements, structural design, and application‐specific thermal management across buildings, electronics, and enclosed systems.








ABSTRACT
Radiative cooling, featuring zero‐energy operation and compatibility with global decarbonization, is a promising route for passive thermal management. Despite major progress over the past few years, advances in radiative cooling have mainly focused on spectral modulation, while the role of thermal conduction in determining practical cooling performance remains far less systematically understood. In fact, different thermal conduction modes can influence radiative cooling in distinct ways by either limiting parasitic heat gain from the environment or enabling heat dissipation from internal sources. Accordingly, radiative cooling materials need to be systematically examined through the lens of tailored thermal conduction. Here, we first analyze the coupling mechanisms between radiative cooling and three different thermal‐conduction modes, namely thermal insulation, enhanced heat conduction, and thermal rectification, and further quantitatively clarify the effects of thermal conduction under different operating conditions, together with the distinct roles of in‐plane and through‐plane thermal transport and system‐level thermal resistance. Building on these mechanisms, we survey recent developments in thermo‐optically engineered radiative cooling materials and their implementation. We further discuss the potential of these different coupling mechanisms in diverse applications. Finally, we identify unresolved challenges and promising research directions for advancing radiative cooling technologies with tailored thermal conduction.

title: Photothermal‐Seek: Literature‐Grounded Knowledge Graphs for Discovering High‐Performance Solar Evaporators
content:
Photothermal‐Seek integrates a literature‐grounded knowledge graph with a document database to convert scattered solar interfacial evaporation (SIE) reports into traceable design knowledge. Semantic‐space analysis identifies conjugated–carbonaceous/fibrous hybrids as promising architectures. Guided by this rule, PPy@DW/CP achieves 2.275  kg·m−2·h−1, while held‐out validation supports early assessment of unseen evaporator designs.








ABSTRACT
Solar interfacial evaporation (SIE) offers a low‐energy route for desalination and water purification, but high‐performance evaporator design still relies heavily on experience. Here, we report Photothermal‐Seek, a literature‐grounded and evidence‐anchored knowledge framework that connects synthesis, structure, and performance information in SIE materials. Built from 2771 publications, Photothermal‐Seek integrates large language model (LLM)‐assisted extraction, graph‐based reasoning, and full‐text retrieval of source evidence, generating a knowledge base with 57 707 nodes, 126 649 relationships, and 1535 curated material nodes. Repeated object‐level audits showed that most sampled extracted objects were supported by source evidence, while benchmark evaluation demonstrated improved domain‐specific reasoning relative to general‐purpose language models. Literature‐scale semantic analysis shows that conjugated materials had the largest representation in the corpus‐defined upper evaporation‐rate tertile, while multicomponent systems near the conjugated–carbonaceous/fibrous semantic boundary emerged as candidates for further investigation. Guided by this rule, we built and tested a polypyrrole‐coated delignified wood evaporator with a cellulose nanofiber/poly(vinyl alcohol) capillary‐regulation layer (PPy@DW/CP), which achieved 2.275 kg·m−2·h−1. A held‐out Dyson sphere‐like evaporator (DSE‐V) case further supports performance estimation for unseen evaporator designs. These results show that literature‐grounded knowledge graphs can connect reported SIE knowledge with real material design and support the early assessment of new evaporator systems.

title: Engineered IFN‐γ‐Expressing Platelet‐Like Microparticles Trigger Macrophage‐Targeted Immunity to Eradicate Liver Metastases
content:
Engineered IFN‐γ‐expressing platelet‐like microparticles functionalized with a hepatic macrophage‐targeting peptide enable localized cytokine delivery to liver macrophages. This macrophage‐directed immunomodulation enhances CXCR6+ and CD8+ T‐cell recruitment and effector responses, thereby suppressing colorectal cancer liver metastases.








ABSTRACT
Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer liver metastasis is often compromised by a highly immunosuppressive hepatic microenvironment characterized by tolerogenic macrophages that act as a systemic immune sink. Here, given the potent but systemically toxic antitumor profile of interferon‐γ (IFN‐γ), we engineered hepatic macrophage‐targeted cytokine‐expressing platelet‐like microparticles (HM‐CPMP) for the local delivery of IFN‐γ, thereby reprogramming the immune status of the liver. Mechanistically, HM‐CPMP treatment drove extensive M1‐like macrophage polarization and a CXCL9/10 chemotactic axis, which together shifted the liver from a tolerogenic to a pro‐inflammatory state. Therefore, systemic administration of HM‐CPMP facilitated the clearance of established liver metastases and conferred a marked survival benefit while strictly preserving systemic homeostasis. Intravital imaging revealed that this localized innate immune reprogramming broke the immunosuppressive tumor niche and recruited polyfunctional CXCR6+ and CD8+ T cells to eradicate metastatic cells. Collectively, by enabling precise hepatic immune modulation, the cytokine‐expressing platelet‐like microparticle delivery platform unleashes a potent localized antitumor response while preserving systemic homeostasis. Our findings provide a highly translational clinical strategy for biosynthetic cytokine‐based immunotherapy against liver metastases.

title: Harnessing Multi‐Effect Coupling for Deep‐Level Trap Engineering in Graphene/Liquid Crystal Polymer Composites Toward High‐Fidelity Electrostatic Loudspeakers
content:
This work reports a microstructural regulation strategy using π–π interactions between liquid crystal polymer and multilayer graphene, alongside a fluorinated liquid crystal surface layer, to construct 1.8 eV deep‐level charge traps. The resulting electrostatic loudspeaker achieves 91.4 dB SPL (@775 Hz) and <0.53% THD (3–20 kHz), offering a bias‐free, high‐fidelity solution for flexible consumer and automotive acoustic transducers.








ABSTRACT
Electrostatic loudspeakers (ESLs) demand lightweight, robust diaphragms with stable high‐density charge storage, yet conventional electrets suffer from rapid charge dissipation, shallow trap levels, and severe environmental sensitivity. This work reports a microstructural regulation strategy based on the strong interaction between liquid crystal polymer (LCP) and multilayer graphene (MLG), combined with fluorinated liquid crystals (F‐LC). The strong π–π stacking interaction between the rigid mesogenic units of LCP and MLG modulates the band structure of MLG and induces Maxwell–Wagner–Sillars (MWS) interfacial polarization. It constructs deep‐level charge traps and increases the density of charge traps. The strong electrostatic attraction of F‐LC enhances charge‐trapping capability and improves the hydrophobicity of the composite, delivering superior environmental stability. Thermally stimulated discharge current (TSDC) measurements confirm a trap energy level of 1.8 eV, with an average absolute surface potential of 8.7 kV. The resulting electrostatic loudspeaker achieves a maximum sound pressure level (SPL) of 91.4 dB at 775 Hz and extremely low total harmonic distortion (THD < 0.53%) over a wide frequency range (3–20 kHz). This work provides a promising pathway for high‐fidelity, bias‐free flexible acoustic transducers, overcoming the long‐standing bottleneck for ESLs in consumer and automotive applications.

title: Strain‐Tolerant Layered Oxide Cathode for Sodium‐Ion Batteries Enabled by a Coherent Perovskite Phase
content:
Rapid Na+ extraction induces lattice strain and structural degradation in layered transition‐metal oxide cathodes. To address this issue, a coherently intergrown perovskite Ca2MnO4 (CMO) phase is introduced to serve a strain‐buffering role. By suppressing localized structural over‐expansion, this composite architecture promotes a more homogeneous distribution of lattice strain and thereby improves the high‐rate cycling stability.








ABSTRACT
Sodium‐ion batteries are considered strong contenders for high‐rate and high‐power energy storage owing to their favorable ion‐transport kinetics. However, under rapid Na+ (de)intercalation, layered oxide cathodes are prone to highly non‐uniform Na+ extraction, which readily induces pronounced lattice strain accumulation, triggering heterogeneous phase evolution, crack formation, and progressive structural degradation, ultimately limiting rate capability and cycling stability. Despite extensive efforts devoted to compositional optimization and surface modification, an intrinsic and structure‐level strategy for directly regulating rate‐dependent strain evolution in layered oxide cathodes remains elusive. Here, by introducing a coherently intergrown perovskite Ca2MnO4 phase into a layered NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 framework, a strain‐tolerant composite architecture is rationally constructed. The embedded perovskite phase effectively buffers lattice deformation and constrains strain accumulation during rapid Na+ deintercalation, thereby stabilizing the structural evolution of the layered host. This strain‐buffering design concept provides new insights into lattice‐level regulation in layered oxide cathodes and opens a viable pathway toward the development of high‐rate and long‐life sodium‐ion batteries.

title: Electrically Fueled Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation for Active Transport
content:
An electrically fueled, waste‐free dissipative coacervation platform functions as active carriers, enabling directional transport of diverse cargos including small molecules, biomolecules, and nanoparticles through a Brownian motor‐like mechanism.








ABSTRACT
Out‐of‐equilibrium liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) of biomacromolecules in living cells creates membraneless organelle, enabling diverse functions including active transport. This has inspired the development of synthetic nonequilibrium LLPS systems; however, their active states are often hampered by waste accumulation, and their emergent functional properties remain largely unexplored. Here, we report an electrically fueled dissipative LLPS that sustains active coacervation without waste generation and, most notably, enables the recruitment and directional transport of molecules and nanoparticles via a new mechanism of active transport. By harnessing an electrochemical reaction network, we modulate a redox‐sensitive peptide that rapidly triggers LLPS resulting in dynamic formation and dissipation of coacervates that suppress Ostwald ripening while exhibiting growth, fusion, and sustained homeostasis. The dissipative coacervates function as active carriers that recruit and transport diverse cargos—including organic molecules, biomolecules, and nanoparticles—with spatiotemporal control. Directional cargo transport arises from the interplay of active coacervation, cargo loading, Brownian motion in bulk solution, and spatially biased droplet dissipation and release near the cathode—a mechanism analogous to Brownian motors operating in cells. This work establishes a new paradigm for directional cargo transport via nonequilibrium LLPS, with broad implications for biotechnology, targeted delivery, and environmental remediation.

title: High‐Performance Lithium‐Sulfur All‐Solid–State Batteries Enabled by Chemically Synthesized Lithium Polysulfide Cathodes
content:
A paradox in Li–S all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) concerns the role of lithium polysulfides (LiPS). Here, we chemically synthesize solid LiPS that remain stable at room temperature, enhance charge transport and sulfur utilization, and alter sulfur‐conversion reactions, challenging the prevailing view that lithium polysulfides are unstable in ASSBs.








ABSTRACT
To achieve high specific energy and long lifespan in lithium‐sulfur all solid‐state batteries (Li‐S ASSBs), it is pivotal to ensure high sulfur utilization and minimize volume change during cycling. In this work, we synthesize a partially lithiated sulfur material (S@Li2S) by mechanical mixing sulfur with lithium sulfide (Li2S). To our surprise, characterization techniques including Raman spectroscopy, solid‐state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR), and sulfur K‐edge X‐ray absorption near edge structure spectroscopy (XANES) reveal the formation of lithium polysulfide (Li2Sn) species that can be stabilized at room temperature, previously thought to be unlikely in the solid‐state. With enhanced reactivity, these lithium polysulfide cathode materials show much faster kinetics than S or Li2S and are always present throughout the charge and discharge processes. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations indicate that different polysulfide species have similar densities. This explains the observed minimal volume change of S@Li2S during cycling. Consequently, this cathode delivers a high specific capacity of 780 mAh g−1, more than double that of sulfur (315 mAh g−1), with an 85% capacity retention after 500 cycles. These mechanistic insights and cycling performance advancement contribute to the development of the high‐performance, next‐generation Li‐S ASSBs.

title: Descriptor‐Informed Screening of Interface‐Active Molecules for Efficient Magnesium Metal Anodes
content:
A descriptor‐informed molecular screening strategy identifies 4‐bromo‐N, N‐dimethylaniline (BrNNA) as an interface‐active electrolyte component that enables fast Mg stripping/plating in Mg(TFSI)2‐based electrolytes. By simultaneously regulating Mg2+ solvation and interphase formation, the BrNNA‐containing electrolyte delivers activation‐free Mg electrochemistry with exceptional stability and high‐rate capability.








ABSTRACT
Rechargeable magnesium batteries offer a compelling pathway toward sustainable energy storage, yet realizing this vision demands scalable electrolytes formulated with widely accessible salts, such as magnesium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (Mg(TFSI)2). Progress in Mg(TFSI)2‐based electrolytes has been severely hindered by low Mg stripping/plating efficiency, arising from sluggish Mg2+ desolvation kinetics and uncontrolled interfacial reactions. Herein, we adopt a descriptor‐informed molecular screening approach and identify 4‐bromo‐N, N‐dimethylaniline (BrNNA) as an interface‐active electrolyte component that enables fast Mg stripping/plating kinetics in Mg(TFSI)2‐based electrolytes. Recognizing their relevance to interface modulation, dipole moment, lowest unoccupied molecular orbital energy, and donor number are employed as quantifiable molecular descriptors to screen a series of substituted aniline derivatives, from which BrNNA emerges as the optimal candidate. The optimized BrNNA‐containing electrolyte supports immediate and stable Mg electrochemistry without activation, sustaining over 2400 h at 0.1 mA cm−2 in symmetric cells and achieving cumulative areal capacities up to 5 Ah cm−2 at 10 mA cm−2. We reveal that BrNNA participates in Mg2+ solvation while preferentially adsorbing onto the Mg surface, lowering the Mg2+ desolvation barrier and directing the formation of a thin Br‐containing interface that facilitates interfacial Mg2+ transport. Moreover, the electrolyte has been validated in full Mg cells using various cathode materials.

title: Helicity‐Defined Analog Conductance States in Chiral Perovskite Synapses
content:
Chiral perovskite synapses convert the handedness of circularly polarized light into persistent analog memory during electrical programming. An optimized n = 3 structure combines strong helicity selectivity with low read noise, enabling 72 distinct conductance levels. These helicity‐programmed states remain readable in a 7 × 7 array, demonstrating optical handedness as a practical hardware memory signal.








ABSTRACT
Optoelectronic synapses encode light through scalar variables (i.e., intensity or wavelength), leaving inputs that differ only in field symmetry indistinguishable at the hardware level. Circularly polarized light introduces helicity as a symmetry‐defined degree of freedom; however, the conversion into persistent analog memory remains challenging. This study demonstrates that optical helicity biases the electrically driven formation of persistent analog conductance states in chiral quasi‐two‐dimensional perovskite synapses. Within the (R/S‐PEA)2MAn‐1PbnI3n+1 multi‐quantum‐well series, the n = 3 composition provided the optimal convergence of chiroptical selectivity, layered structural registry, and transport‐supporting structural order, enabling reproducible low‐nonlinearity analog weight updates and 72 statistically distinguishable conductance states retained over 106 s. An independently evaluated read‐noise‐informed framework yielded a read‐noise‐limited capacity estimate of 72.3 levels, providing a quantitative link between measured read noise and analog‐state capacity. In conclusion, optical helicity can be encoded into, retained in, and read from electrically programmed analog conductance states, providing a persistent state variable for neuromorphic computation.

title: Physics‐Guided Active Learning Enables Energy‐Filtering Flexible Thermoelectric Composites for Self‐Powered Wound Bioelectronics
content:
Physics‐guided active learning workflow for designing energy‐filtering flexible thermoelectric composites.








ABSTRACT
Thermoelectric stimulation offers a self‐powered intervention for accelerated wound healing by converting physiological thermal gradients into sustained micro‐electric fields. However, the development of flexible thermoelectric materials is constrained by the coupled dependence of electrical conductivity and the Seebeck coefficient, which empirical screening alone is inefficient for exploring the large number of possible interfaces. We developed a small‐data, literature‐derived, physics‐guided screening and design framework that integrates Bayesian optimization with eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) regression and subsequent experimental validation. Using 18 physics‐informed descriptors selected by recursive feature elimination, the framework predicts interfacial energy barriers within the literature‐derived data domain with a test R2 of 0.87, enabling targeted barrier engineering that partially decouples the thermoelectric parameters. The model and practical screening criteria were used to select five composite systems for synthesis and experimental evaluation, supporting the applicability of the algorithm. Among the experimentally validated systems, poly(3,4‐ethylenedioxythiophene): poly(styrene sulfonate)/eutectic gallium‐indium (PEDOT:PSS/EGaIn) flexible composite exhibited a measured interfacial energy barrier of 0.24 eV, close to the predicted effective filtering range, and achieved a Seebeck coefficient of 40.0 µV K−1. Under a mild physiological‐to‐ambient temperature gradient of 25 K, the flexible thermoelectric device generated an open‐circuit voltage of 8.80 mV. In the scratch assay, the stimulated group showed 34.5% closure compared with 13.9% in the untreated control. In the rat wound model, the thermoelectric group reached near‐complete closure approximately two days earlier than the sham and untreated groups. This data‐driven approach provides a physical framework for screening energy‐filtering composites and evaluating their potential in self‐powered bioelectronic therapeutics.

title: Bridge‐Atom Connected Tiny‐Nanosheet Driven Delocalized Electron Transfer on Graphene for 2‐Electron Oxygen Reduction Reaction
content:
Semi‐continuous tiny graphene (SCTG) was fabricated via isothermal molten‐self‐assembly strategy. Its bridge‐connected nanosheets confine delocalized electrons, reduce dissipation and optimize charge density, boosting oxygen adsorption and charge transfer for efficient 2e− ORR.








ABSTRACT
Metal‐free graphene‐based materials are promising alternatives to precious‐metal catalysts in the 2‐electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e− ORR). While previous research has highlighted the critical role of charge density at active sites, the precise controlling the charge transfer via structural engineering on metal‐free graphene remains elusive. In this work, we construct a semi‐continuous tiny graphene (SCTG) architecture by a novel isothermal molten‐self‐assembly strategy, which is composed of nanosized graphene sheets interconnected by a sparse number of bridge atoms. This unique arrangement offers dual advantages: the high density of edge atoms in the small graphene domains facilitates the generation and retention of delocalized electrons, while the minimal bridge atoms reduce electron dissipation pathways, ensuring efficient charge delivery to reactive sites. Notably, this configuration balances electron confinement and mobility—preserving necessary charge routes without enabling excessive leakage. As a result, the SCTG structure elevates the local charge density at catalytic sites to an optimal level, enhancing both oxygen adsorption and electron transfer kinetics. This culminates in a remarkable ORR selectivity of 100% and a production rate of 13.3 mol g−1 h−1 for H2O2. These findings offer valuable insight into how graphene‐based structures can be fine‐tuned for precise electron control in electrocatalysis.

title: Differential Sedimentation and Cryo‐TEM Mapping Resolve Structural Heterogeneity in Conjugated Polymer Nanowires for Programmable Stretchable Electronics
content:
Density‐driven differential sedimentation fractionates solution‐assembled P3HT nanowires into crystalline and disordered constituents. High‐resolution cryo‐TEM directly visualizes the molecular chain packing within individual nanowires in real space, and recombining the fractions programs the mobility–stretchability trade‐off without chemical modification, reframing intrinsic structural heterogeneity as a quantitative design parameter for stretchable electronics.








ABSTRACT
The performance of stretchable electronics based on semicrystalline conjugated polymers (CPs) is determined by the balance between crystalline order and interdomain connectivity provided by amorphous tie molecules, rather than by crystallinity alone. Solution‐state crystallization‐driven self‐assembly (CDSA) of CPs into nanowires (NWs) enables solution‐processable thin films without post‐deposition annealing to enhance crystallinity. In cast films, crystalline NWs provide charge‐transport pathways, whereas non‐aggregated amorphous chains bridge adjacent NW crystallites, sustain interdomain charge percolation, and accommodate mechanical deformation. Yet this assembly inevitably yields heterogeneous mixtures of crystalline NWs and amorphous chains, which resist single‐NW quantification and independent control. In this study, density‐driven differential sedimentation fractionates poly(3‐hexylthiophene) (P3HT) NWs into a sediment of crystalline NWs and a supernatant of shorter NWs and lower‐molecular‐weight chains. Cryo‐TEM quantitative morphological mapping resolves backbone tilt, width uniformity, and lamellar coherence at the single‐NW level, showing that local cofacial π–π packing is preserved in both fractions whereas long‐range order along the lamellar stacking direction is concentrated in the sediment. Recombining the fractions at controlled weight ratios tunes the mobility–stretchability trade‐off without chemical modification, and the strategy generalizes to coaxial p–n heterojunction hybrid NWs of P3HT‐b‐poly(2‐vinylpyridine)/CdSe quantum dots formed by CDSA, reframing structural heterogeneity as a programmable design parameter for stretchable electronics.

title: Elastic Ion‐Conducting Layer Enables Stable Si‐Based All‐Solid‐State Batteries
content:
An elastic ion‐conducting layer simultaneously enhances interfacial mechanical adaptability and lithium‐ion transport kinetics in silicon anodes for sulfide‐based all‐solid‐state batteries, stabilizing both electrode integrity and solid‐solid interfacial contact with sulfide solid electrolytes. As a result, the resulting full cell achieves an ultralong cycling life of 10,000 cycles at 5C, while pouch cell sustains stable operation over 650 cycles.








ABSTRACT
Si‐based all‐solid‐state batteries with sulfide solid electrolytes are strong contenders for next‐generation high‐safety, high‐energy‐density batteries. However, Si‐based anodes inevitably suffer from irreversible delamination and side reactions at the rigid Si/solid electrolyte interface during cycling, making it challenging to achieve long cycle life. Here, we develop an elastic ion‐conducting layer on the Si surface that transforms the rigid interface into a conformal and recoverable elastic contact, achieving highly stable Si anode. The layer comprises a lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide‐containing block copolymer, whose hydrogen‐bond‐rich hard domains provide mechanical robustness and elasticity. Ion‐conductive soft segments, together with an in situ‐formed inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase on the Si surface, construct a three‐dimensional ion transport network. This interfacial architecture simultaneously mitigates interfacial stress and accelerates lithium‐ion transport within the Si anode. Consequently, the full‐cell exhibits stable cycling over 10,000 cycles at a high rate of 5C (8.7 mA cm−2), and the 0.6 Ah pouch cell retains 91% capacity after 650 cycles. Such interfacial layer holds great promise for accelerating the commercialization of Si‐based all‐solid‐state batteries.

title: Quantum Hall Effect in Stoichiometry‐Engineered β$\beta$‐Ag2Te${\rm Ag}_2{\rm Te}$
content:
Precise Te‐capping control enables systematic tuning of carrier density and mobility in epitaxial β$\beta$‐Ag2Te${\rm Ag}_2{\rm Te}$ thin films. An optimized Te overlayer suppresses excess electron doping while preserving high mobility, driving the system toward the intrinsic transport regime. The resulting carrier‐density–mobility evolution reveals the exceptional electronic quality of β$\beta$‐Ag2Te${\rm Ag}_2{\rm Te}$ and establishes surface stoichiometry engineering as an effective route to tailor topological transport.








ABSTRACT
Accessing surface quantum transport in topological insulators is hampered by residual bulk conduction arising from lattice defects. Here, we demonstrate a novel synthesis pathway for realizing high‐mobility β$\beta$‐Ag2Te${\rm Ag}_2{\rm Te}$ thin films in which surface transport is dominant. An in situ room‐temperature Te treatment modifies the film stoichiometry, enabling continuous tuning of the sheet carrier density over more than an order of magnitude through the charge‐neutrality point without an external gate electrode. In the lower‐carrier‐density films, a fully developed ν=1$\nu =1$ quantum Hall state is observed, and Landau‐level energies extracted across samples collapse onto the EN=vF2eℏNB$E_N=v_\mathrm{F}\sqrt {2e\hbar NB}$ relation, providing evidence for the massless Dirac dispersion of the top and bottom surface states. These results establish stoichiometry engineering as a lithography‐ and gate‐free approach to accessing quantum Hall transport in epitaxial topological‐insulator thin films.
