title: Simultaneous Laser Light and Electromagnetic Wave Pulsed Emissions Triggered by Spatiotemporally‐Compressed Triboelectricity
content:
Leveraging a spatiotemporally‐compressed instantaneous discharging mechanism, a self‐powered radiator synchronously emits laser light (LL) and electromagnetic waves (EWs). This dual‐mode paradigm enables a theoretically estimated wireless communication distance exceeding 3300 meters. By modulating the complementary radiations, the system enables maintenance‐free, real‐time monitoring of multidimensional environmental factors, including environmental motions, water contamination, the presence of metal, and gas or liquid components.








ABSTRACT
Serving as information carriers, laser light (LL) and electromagnetic waves (EWs) lay the foundation of information sensing and communication systems for modern society, featuring different advantages and disadvantages. Simultaneously emitting LL and EWs with environmental information modulated in a self‐powered manner has great potential to benefit diverse applications, especially internet of things (IoTs). In this work, a triboelectricity‐driven radiator is developed for simultaneous emissions of LL and EWs. Driven by the environmental motion‐induced triboelectricity, the LL and EW emissions are achieved by the breakdown‐induced discharging via a tailored instantaneous charge transfer channel where the spatially accumulated charge is released within an ultrashort time. At least 5 environmental factors, including environmental motion profiles, concentrations of pollutants, gas components, liquid types, and the presence of metal, can be sensed and wirelessly transmitted. The information interaction can be operated in two modes, isotropic EWs and collimated LL. Attributed to the spatiotemporally‐compressed triboelectric mechanism, the generated ultrahigh current of 11 A drives the simultaneous LL and EW radiations for multidimensional sensing, achieving a highly competitive Figure‐of‐Merit of 100. Our results demonstrate a proof‐of‐concept of the all‐in‐one information system enabled by the TENG, paving a new avenue to achieve TENG‐based multiple‐environmental‐factor sensing.

title: Leveraging Rh in Mixed Pt/Rh Streams Enables Activity–Durability Synergy in PtCo Intermetallic Fuel Cell Catalysts
content:
Compositionally informed direct upcycling converts a Pt/Rh mixed solution into ordered Rh–PtCo/C without prior Pt/Rh separation. Predicted subsurface Rh tunes Pt surface reactivity and strengthens alloy bonding, enabling an initial H2–air peak power density of 1.12 W cm−2 and 95.54% retention after 30 000 membrane–electrode–assembly cycles, while scenario analyses indicate reduced environmental impacts and processing costs.








ABSTRACT
Ordered PtCo intermetallic catalysts are promising oxygen reduction catalysts for proton exchange membrane fuel cells, but simultaneously achieving high activity, durability, and sustainable platinum group metal (PGM) utilization remains challenging. Here, literature‐scale composition mapping and density functional theory screening are combined to identify Rh as a functional regulator of PtCo, leading to a compositionally informed synthesis of ordered Rh–PtCo/C from a Pt/Rh mixed solution. Structural characterization supports Rh incorporation into the PtCo framework, while cluster expansion calculations predict preferential subsurface enrichment. The predicted subsurface Rh configuration downshifts the Pt d‐band center, moderates oxygenated‐intermediate binding, and strengthens the internal metal–metal bonding network. Rh–PtCo/C consequently delivers a mass activity of 1.792 A mgPt−1 and a total‐PGM‐normalized activity of 1.59 A mgPGM−1 at 0.9 V versus RHE. In H2–air membrane electrode assemblies, it reaches a peak power density of 1.12 W cm−2 and retains 95.54% of its initial value after 30 000 voltage cycles. Scenario‐based life cycle assessment and techno‐economic analysis further indicate that retaining coexisting Rh may reduce downstream processing burdens compared with separation‐intensive Pt/Rh routes. This work establishes compositionally informed subsurface regulation for coupling high‐performance intermetallic catalyst design with the value‐retaining use of mixed‐metal resources.

title: Glass Transition of Chiral Hybrid Metal Halides for Self‐Supported 3D Printing
content:
A thermal programming strategy for multi‐dimensional manufacturing of chiral hybrid metal halides (HMHs) was established by integrating their intrinsic crystal‐melt‐glass transition with 3D printing technology. The printed glass structures retained high‐efficiency linear optical photoluminescence and strong isotropic nonlinear optical second harmonic generation, providing valuable design principles for developing HMH glasses with a stable thermal processing window.








ABSTRACT
Hybrid metal halides (HMHs) have emerged as promising functional materials owing to their versatile structural tunability and outstanding optoelectronic properties. In particular, chiral HMHs could be endowed with fascinating chiroptoelectronic properties such as circularly polarized light emission, circularly polarized photodetection, and spin regulation. However, the implementation of their practical integrated optoelectronic applications has been mainly restricted to planar thin‐film devices due to the poor processability of chiral HMHs for the construction of complex three‐dimensional (3D) architectures. Here, we take advantage of the glass transition of chiral HMH with 3D printing technology to construct self‐supported 3D architectures with high‐performance linear and nonlinear optical functionalities. Chiral HMH (R/S‐THNA)3SbCl6·0.5H2O (R/S‐THNA = R/S‐1,2,3,4‐tetrahydro‐1‐naphthylammonium) forms transparent amorphous glass upon rapid quenching from its molten state. The resulting R/S‐SbCl‐glass favors tunable photoluminescence colors and a large, continuously tunable range of glass transition temperature (∼50°C) through metal halide infusion. The intrinsic thermoplasticity of HMH glasses allows for additive‐free, thermally assisted extrusion‐based printing of self‐supporting 3D architectures. Upon recrystallization, the printed structures recovered non‐centrosymmetric crystal lattices and exhibited strong isotropic second harmonic generation response, enabling customized nonlinear optical imaging. This work establishes a thermally programmable paradigm for transforming HMHs from molecularly designed materials into 3D optical architectures.

title: Fe3+‐Triggered Scalable Slow‐Corrosion Engineering for Industrial Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis at 2.0 A cm−2
content:
A new type of mechanically ultra‐stable alkaline self‐supported oxygen evolution electrocatalyst, overcoming the long‐standing issue of catalyst layer delamination and deactivation under ampere‐level current densities that plagues conventional powder catalysts and those synthesized via hydrothermal or electrodeposition routes.








ABSTRACT
The practical application of anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) is hindered by the lack of durable anodes for industrial‐scale current densities (≥ 1000 mA cm−2). Herein, we report a scalable Fe3+‐triggered homogeneous slow‐corrosion strategy to fabricate a Fe‐doped Ni(OH)2/NiS hybrid on nickel foam (Fe‐Ni(OH)2/NiS/NF) for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). This approach couples the slow corrosion of Ni foam by Fe3+ with the in situ nucleation of the Fe‐Ni(OH)2/NiS hybrid, creating a seamless, interface‐free integration with exceptional mechanical adhesion. The optimized Fe‐Ni(OH)2/NiS/NF electrode exhibits exceptional stability for over 1100 h at ampere‐level current densities up to 2000 mA cm−2 without performance decay. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the catalyst undergoes rapid reconstruction at low potentials to form an amorphous Ni(Fe)OOH layer, which serves as the true active phase and primarily follows the adsorbate evolution mechanism, thereby avoiding the chemical degradation associated with lattice oxygen participation. Density functional theory calculations indicate that Fe doping upshifts the NiOOH d‐band center, strengthening *OH adsorption and thus lowering the *OH→*O barrier to accelerate OER kinetics. In an AEMWE, it requires only 1.706 and 1.852 V to achieve 1.0 and 2.0 A cm−2, respectively, maintaining stable operation at industrial currents for over 1800 h.

title: Cooperative Assembly Drives Buried Interface Engineering for Efficient Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
A synergistically assembled chemically heterogeneous interface integrates Me‐4PACz with carbazole‐9‐ethanol to regulate molecular organization and buried‐interface chemistry in inverted perovskite solar cells. Heteromolecular interactions suppress excessive Me‐4PACz self‐association, while the hydroxyethyl functionality promotes interfacial passivation, enabling 27.06% efficiency (26.86% certified) and 21.90% efficiency in 30 × 30 cm2 modules.








ABSTRACT
Self‐assembled monolayers (SAMs) containing carbazole and phosphonic acid groups have emerged as effective hole‐transport layers (HTLs) for high‐performance inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, the intrinsic aggregation tendency of SAM molecules often compromises interfacial uniformity, inducing non‐radiative recombination and limiting device efficiency and stability. Here, we report a synergistically assembled chemically heterogeneous (SACH) interfacial layer constructed by integrating [4‐(3,6‐dimethyl‐9H‐carbazol‐9‐yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (Me‐4PACz) with carbazole‐9‐ethanol (CE). In this strategy, CE promotes favorable heteromolecular π‐associated and dispersion interactions with Me‐4PACz, thereby moderating excessive Me‐4PACz self‐association, improving interfacial uniformity, and enhancing charge extraction. Meanwhile, the hydroxyl group of CE supports an O─H···I− interaction with perovskite, contributing to interfacial defect passivation and suppressed buried‐interface recombination. As a result, devices employing the SACH layer achieve a PCE of 27.06% (certified 26.86%). Under maximum power point tracking in ambient air at 65°C, encapsulated SACH‐based devices retained 88.6% of their initial efficiency after 500 h. Large‐area perovskite modules (30 × 30 cm2) further demonstrate promising performance with an efficiency of 21.90%, highlighting the broad applicability of this cooperative interfacial design for scalable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Tailoring Fluorinated Chain Positioning in Anion Exchange Membranes for Boosted Ion and Water Transport Channels
content:
A tailored fluorinated chain strategy is developed to resolve the trade‐off between hydration‐driven electrolytic performance and dimensional instability caused by swelling in anion exchange membranes. This structural engineering optimizes amphiphilic self‐assembly to establish enhanced ion and water transport channels. The resulting PTAfcP membrane achieves high alkaline conductivity, enabling high device performance and robust long‐term stability in water electrolyzers. 








ABSTRACT
Anion exchange membranes (AEMs) have advanced anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs) by achieving high ionic conductivity and controlled swelling, yet balancing hydration‐enhanced electrolytic performance and swelling‐induced dimensional instability remains a key challenge for scalable application. In this work, we advance beyond conventional cationic grafting modification strategies via the rational design of fluorinated alkyl side chains on hydrophobic polymer backbones, thereby enhancing amphiphilic self‐assembly. Such structural engineering facilitates the formation of interconnected pathways that enable efficient hydroxide ion and water transport. The resulting PTAfcP membrane exhibits a low swelling ratio of 14.38% and an OH− conductivity of 179.2 mS cm−1 at 80°C. Notably, the establishment of an efficient alkaline electrolyte transport network enables the PTAfcP‐based electrolyzer to achieve a current density of 7.5 A cm−2. Furthermore, the electrolyzer incorporating a PTAfcP membrane demonstrates satisfactory durability over 2000 h of operation, exhibiting a voltage fade rate of only 17.9 µV h−1 at 0.5 A cm−2, substantiating its application potential for industrial‐scale deployment.

title: Hierarchical Chemical Ordering Enables Ultra‐Efficient Strengthening and Multifunctionality
content:
Breaking the long‐standing strength–functionality trade‐off, hierarchical chemical ordering transforms grain boundaries sliding softening into ultra‐efficient hardening. Only 0.17 at.% solute (Zn‐0.12Mg‐0.05Mn) enables a record 350 MPa yield strength, demonstrating a new route toward ultra‐lean, multifunctional metallic materials.








ABSTRACT
Modern alloy design increasingly seeks substantial strengthening with minimal alloying to improve sustainability while preserving or enhancing matrix functionality, an imperative for high‐end applications like biodegradable implants. Yet for over half a century, strengthening has relied on introducing intensive defects via heavy alloying to impede dislocations; unfortunately, those defects inevitably induce functional degradation, producing a persistent strength‐functionality trade‐off. Here, we transform grain boundary (GB) sliding, typically a source of softening, into an ultra‐efficient strengthening mechanism via engineered hierarchical chemical ordering (HCO). In a model biodegradable near‐pure Zn alloy with only 0.17 at.% solute (Zn‐0.12Mg‐0.05Mn), yield strength increases tenfold to 350 MPa and represents the largest gain for ultra‐lean alloys below 0.5 at.% while exceeding clinical benchmarks. The alloy delivers 32% elongation and uniform biodegradation that exceeds even what was long considered exclusive to pure metals, with 10%–37% higher cell viability, 38% enhanced wound healing, and uncompromised electrical conductivity. The HCO achieves dual‐range strengthening as intragranular Mn‐rich nanoclusters elevate GB motion stress by ∼164% through long‐range suppression of stress relaxation, while Mg segregation at GBs increases critical sliding stress by ∼600% via short‐range pinning. This mechanism bypasses traditional strength‐functionality trade‐offs, establishing a new design paradigm for ultra‐lean, high‐performance alloys.

title: Breaking Lithium Embrittlement in Alloy Anodes Enables Low‐Stack‐Pressure All‐Solid‐State Batteries
content:
Rapid solidification produces a nanoscale, uniformly distributed Sn–In two‐phase microstructure that forms abundant amorphous domains during lithiation. The resulting amorphous‐rich Li–alloy mitigates the mechanical constraints associated with directional bonding in intermetallic compounds, enhances plastic deformability, and preserves solid–solid contact, enabling stable cycling of In–, Sn–, and Al–based alloy anodes at stack pressures reduced from ≥30 to ≤5 MPa.








ABSTRACT
Alloy anodes (Si, Al, In, and Sn) are exceptionally promising for realizing dendrite‐free, high‐energy‐density all‐solid‐state lithium‐ion batteries (ASSLIBs). However, even soft metals such as Al, Sn, and In form hard and brittle lithiated intermetallics upon lithiation, requiring commercially impractical stack pressures during operation. Here, we overcome limited dislocation slip in lithiated intermetallics arising from directional covalent bonding by introducing a nanoscale amorphous structure during lithiation. This mitigates the high hardness and brittleness of lithiated alloys, reducing the required stack pressure for alloy anodes from ≥30 to ≤5 MPa. The results reveal that atomically mixed In and Sn generate abundant nanoscale amorphous structures during lithiation, as mutual lattice disruption suppresses long‐range crystallization. This amorphization facilitates inter‐unit sliding and mitigates the effects of directional covalent bonding in intermetallics, thereby reducing their inherent hardness and brittleness. Consequently, the NMC83|LPSCl|(InSn4)0.64·(In3Sn)0.36 cell (cathode areal loading: 22.37 mg cm−2) delivers 84.3% capacity retention over 2000 cycles at 4.0 C. After incorporating (InSn4)0.64(In3Sn)0.36 composite into Si anode, the NMC83||Si full cell sustains over 400 cycles at 5 MPa and is further validated in pouch cells. This strategy of breaking lithium embrittlement can also be extended to other alloy anodes (Al–, Sb–, and Bi–containing alloy) in ASSLIBs.

title: Vacancy‐Mediated Sulfur Exchange Between Catalysts and Polysulfides Accelerates Sulfur Redox Kinetics in Lithium‐Sulfur Batteries
content:
Accessible sulfur vacancies are revealed as dynamic exchange centers that mediate sulfur transfer between metal sulfide catalysts and polysulfides in lithium‐sulfur batteries. Using Bi2S3 as a model catalyst, vacancy‐mediated sulfur exchange accelerates interfacial sulfur reconstruction and redox kinetics, establishing a catalyst design principle for high‐performance lithium‐sulfur batteries.








ABSTRACT
Metal sulfides are promising sulfur electrocatalysts for lithium‐sulfur (Li–S) batteries, yet their rational design is limited by an incomplete understanding of interfacial sulfur redox processes. Here, we reveal a vacancy‐mediated sulfur‐exchange mechanism that accelerates sulfur redox kinetics. Using Bi2S3 as a model catalyst, 34S isotope‐labeling reveals dynamic sulfur exchange between external polysulfides and vacancy‐associated Bi–S lattice environments during cycling. Accessible sulfur vacancies act as exchange centers, enabling sulfur incorporation, migration, and local reconstruction. By tuning vacancy concentration, we establish a direct correlation between sulfur‐vacancy density, sulfur‐exchange extent, and catalytic sulfur conversion. Vacancy‐rich Bi2S3 nearly doubles the electrochemically accessible interfacial area, with double‐layer capacitance increasing from 1.04 to 2.18 mF cm−2, and raises sulfur exchange from 0.71% to 1.05%. Consequently, Li2S nucleation and precipitation are accelerated; the apparent Li2S formation barrier decreases from 0.352 to 0.179 eV, and polarization and impedance growth are suppressed. A 2.5 Ah Li–S pouch cell delivers an energy density of ∼504 Wh kg−1. These findings identify vacancy‐mediated sulfur exchange as a mechanistic basis for designing high‐performance metal sulfide catalysts for practical sulfur batteries.

title: Sunlight‐Driven Gram‐Scale Nitrate Reduction to Ammonia by an In Situ Formed Fe3+1‐xFe2+xOOH/CdSeS Photocatalyst
content:
An outdoor sunlight‐driven photocatalytic system efficiently reduces nitrate to ammonia. Using a 625 cm2 plate ‐ type reactor, the system achieves a high production rate of 72 mmol g−1 h−1 and demonstrates robust stability over 115 h of cumulative operation across 5 cycles, yielding 177.18 mmol of NH3 and 7.83 g of NH4Cl solid under sunlight.








ABSTRACT
Sunlight‐driven conversion of NO3−‐to‐NH3 holds immense significance for fostering a green and sustainable society. However, most of the existing photocatalysts have weak light absorption and a wide band gap, making the synthesis of NH3 challenging on a large scale under sunlight. Herein, a photocatalyst Fe3+1‐xFe2+xOOH/CdSeS that was in situ formed from MPA‐CdSe QDs and transition metal ions (i.e., Fe3+ used here) under visible light irradiation at room temperature, accomplished a gram‐scale synthesis of NH3 in a 625 cm2 plate‐type reactor. Under sunlight, 177.18 mmol NH3 was synthesized, and 7.83 g of NH4Cl solid was collected after five cycles totaling 115 h, and the solar‐to‐ammonia (STA) was 0.664%. Experimental characterization and density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the formation of Fe3+1‐xFe2+xOOH/CdSeS nanostructures is the key to the exceptional activity. The reversible Fe3+/Fe2+ redox cycling within the clusters facilitates charge separation and interfacial transfer from CdSeS QDs to Fe3+1‐xFe2+xOOH under irradiation, while oxygen vacancies in Fe3+1‐xFe2+xOOH clusters bind NO3− for subsequent NH3 formation. The apparent quantum yield is 15.89% ± 1.75% at 436 nm, and the yield of NH3 is 522.47 mmol gcat−1 h−1 based on Fe3+1‐xFe2+xOOH/CdSeS photocatalyst, a 5.82‐fold enhancement over the reported record of 89.79 mmol gcat−1 h−1, demonstrating remarkable application potential for sunlight‐driven NO3− reduction to NH3.

title: Charge‐Reversed Lipid Nanoparticles Enable Encapsulation of Pt2L4 Nanocages for In vivo Anti‐Cancer Treatment
content:
Charge‐reversed lipid nanoparticles (revLNPs) enable efficient encapsulation and delivery of cationic Pt2L4 nanocages. Encapsulation preserves potent anticancer activity while improving circulation, reducing vascular leakage, and promoting favorable biodistribution in vivo. In zebrafish xenografts, Pt2L4‐loaded revLNPs induce substantial tumor regression at markedly lower doses than liposomal cisplatin, establishing revLNPs as a versatile platform for cationic inorganic anticancer therapeutics with translational potential.








ABSTRACT
Inorganic anticancer drugs such as cisplatin remain central to chemotherapy but are limited by poor tumor selectivity, rapid clearance, and off‐target toxicity. We recently developed cationic Pt2L4 nanocages with 12‐fold higher anticancer activity than cisplatin in PC‐3M‐Pro4 cells in vitro, but their positive charge causes rapid extravasation and renal clearance in vivo. Here, we re‐engineer lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) into charge‐reversed lipid nanoparticles (revLNPs) capable of efficiently encapsulating cationic Pt2L4 nanocages. Pt2L4‐loaded revLNPs retain high cancer‐cell uptake and cytotoxicity in vitro comparable to the free drug. Following intravenous administration, they show prolonged circulation, reduced vessel‐wall leakage, and favorable biodistribution in zebrafish embryos. In mice, revLNPs exhibit a 1.7‐fold longer plasma half‐life than the clinically approved Onpattro LNP formulation while maintaining characteristic liver and spleen tropism. In zebrafish xenografts, a single injection induces substantial tumor regression, reaching 20% in PC‐3M‐Pro4 and 72% in MDA‐MB‐231 tumors, and outperforms Lipocisplatin despite a ten‐fold lower therapeutic dose. These results establish revLNPs as a broadly applicable delivery platform that overcomes solubility, biodistribution, and pharmacokinetic barriers of cationic inorganic drugs, enabling their effective use in vivo.

title: Breaking Bottlenecks in Solid Electrolyte Discovery With Large Artificial Intelligence Models
content:
Large AI models are presented as a route to break key bottlenecks in solid electrolyte discovery by linking materials databases, machine‐learning interatomic potentials, large language models, and autonomous experiments. This perspective highlights how AI can accelerate the identification of solid electrolytes with fast ion transport, stable interfaces, and robust mechanical properties for better solid‐state batteries.








ABSTRACT
Solid electrolytes (SEs) are central to next‐generation metal batteries, yet their discovery remains constrained by fragmented data, limited transferability of simulations, and slow experimental iteration. Unlike catalysis, where surface reactivity dominates, SEs require simultaneous optimization of bulk ion transport, defect chemistry, mechanical integrity, and interfacial stability. Here, we outline a framework for autonomous SE discovery enabled by large artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and large language models (LLMs). We discuss the evolution from static materials databases to dynamic, self‐updating knowledge systems, the role of MLIPs in bridging density functional theory (DFT) and long‐timescale ion migration, and the emergence of LLMs as engines for literature mining, hypothesis generation, and scientific reasoning. We further describe a closed‐loop architecture integrating AI‐driven candidate design, multiscale simulation, uncertainty‐aware selection, and experimental validation. Such systems shift SE research from intuition‐guided exploration to data‐informed, self‐improving cycles. We conclude by highlighting challenges in data standardization, interfacial complexity, and reproducibility, and we propose design principles for building autonomous laboratories for solid‐state battery materials.

title: Photocatalytic Biomass Valorization: Electronic Polarization Enables Oxygen Activation and Selective C─C Bond Cleavage
content:
Co active‐site engineering and CF3‐induced electronic polarization simultaneously help to endow g‐C3N4 with enhanced interfacial electron transfer and efficient oxygen activation that can be perform under visible‐light irradiation. The generated superoxide radicals (•O2−) promote selective C─C bond cleavage of biomass‐derived carbohydrates, enabling highly selective conversion into formic acid under mild aqueous conditions.








ABSTRACT
Photocatalytic valorization of biomass into value‐added chemicals requires catalysts capable of simultaneously activating molecular oxygen and controlling C─C bond cleavage. In this work, we introduce an electronic polarization engineering strategy by integrating CF3‐induced charge redistribution on Co active‐site regulation in polymeric carbon nitride. It demonstrates that the as‐prepared Co/g‐C3N4‐CF3 photocatalyst enables selective conversion of biomass‐derived carbohydrates into formic acid under visible‐light irradiation and mild aqueous conditions. Mechanistic investigations reveal that ─CF3 functionalization creates localized electronic polarization, while Co sites promote oxygen activation and facilitate the formation of superoxide radicals (•O2−). Density functional theory calculations reveals that this electronic modulation lowers the energetic barrier for the key C─C bond cleavage step. Therefore, this work establishes a general framework for coupling electronic polarization with active‐site engineering to help perform selective oxidation chemistry in solar‐driven catalysis.

title: Hijacking Prenyltransferases and Terpene Synthases for the Enzymatic Synthesis of Non‐natural C19, C24, and C29 Terpenoids
content:
The terpenoid substrate analog 14‐nor‐FPP with a removed Me group and IPP were converted with oligoprenyl pyrophosphate synthases and di‐ or sesterterpene synthases to yield non‐natural terpene analogs. In some cases, new cyclisation cascades were entered, leading to products with novel skeletons. Surprisingly, for some enzyme‐substrate combinations, the removal of one carbon atom allows for incorporation of an additional isoprene unit.








ABSTRACT
The terpenoid substrate analog 14‐nor‐farnesyl pyrophosphate (14‐nor‐FPP), lacking the methyl group Me14, was synthesized and enzymatically elongated to 18‐nor‐geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (18‐nor‐GGPP) and 22‐nor‐geranylfarnesyl pyrophosphate (22‐nor‐GFPP) by GGPP synthase (GGPPS) and GFPP synthase (GFPPS), respectively. Downstream conversion with 20 diterpene synthases (DTSs) and 10 sesterterpene synthases (StTSs) yielded in total 24 new compounds. Surprisingly, in two cases the substrate analogs were converted by GGPPS and a DTS into nor‐sesterterpenes (C24), while one combination of GFPPS and a StTS yielded a nor‐triterpene (C29), demonstrating that the lack of just one carbon allows for extension with one more terpene unit than expected, in contrast to the strict product selectivity observed for GGPPS and GFPPS with normal FPP. For certain enzyme‐substrate pairings, the altered reactivity caused by the absence of Me14 unveiled reaction pathways toward di‐ and sesterterpenes with unique frameworks, for which the mechanisms were investigated through DFT calculations. Absolute configurations of the obtained compounds were determined through chemical correlation with stereoselectively deuterated precursors or through a comparison of optical rotations to those of structurally related natural products containing Me18/Me22.

title: Deferoxamine‐Engineered Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles Unlock High‐Valence Metal Channels for Multiplexed Mass Cytometry
content:
This work developed a chelator‐engineered MSN platform that accommodates four distinct high‐valent metal ions within a common nanoparticle architecture and enables their use as antibody‐conjugated mass tags in multiplexed mass cytometry workflows.








ABSTRACT
Mass cytometry (MC) enables highly multiplexed single‐cell protein analysis, but its full analytical potential remains constrained by the limited range of available mass tags. Here, we report deferoxamine‐engineered mesoporous silica nanoparticles (DFO‐MSNs) for high‐capacity loading of multiple underutilized high‐valent metal ions within a common nanoparticle scaffold. DFO‐MSNs accommodated Zr4+, Hf4+, Nb5+, and Ta5+ at approximately 104 metal atoms per nanoparticle, with high metal retention in physiological buffers. Following PEGylation and antibody (Ab) conjugation, the resulting Zr‐, Nb‐, Hf‐, and Ta‐based probes enabled antigen‐specific detection of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) by co‐staining with commercial Maxpar reagents. Nb‐, Hf‐, and Ta‐loaded MSN_CD8a probes resolved CD8a+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes at titers as low as 30 NPs/cell. In a 30‐plex staining panel, Ta@MSN_CD25 resolved low‐abundance CD25hiCD127lo Treg‐like cells with apparent population recovery comparable to the corresponding Maxpar reagent, while consuming ca. 35‐fold less Ab. Together, these results establish a modular strategy for incorporating underutilized high‐valent metals into functional mass tags and demonstrate the feasibility of integrating MSN‐based probes into multiplexed MC immunophenotyping workflows.

title: Weak‐Solvation Reconstruction of PVDF‐Based Quasi‐Solid‐State Electrolytes Enabling Potassium‐Ion Batteries Working at –5°C
content:
A weak‐solvation reconstruction strategy using sterically hindered triethyl phosphate (TEP) is proposed to optimize conventional PVDF‐based quasi‐solid polymer electrolytes for potassium‐ion batteries. It effectively reshapes the primary solvation sheath and promotes in situ formation of a robust, uniform inorganic‐rich passivation interphase, delivering extended interfacial cycling lifespan and reliable low‐temperature operation at −5°C.








ABSTRACT
Solid‐state potassium‐ion batteries (SSPIBs) promise next‐generation energy storage with abundant resources, intrinsic safety, prolonged cycle life and broad operational temperature ranges. However, their practical application at room temperature is still severely restricted. Although poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF)‐based quasi‐solid‐state electrolytes (SPEs) can achieve room‐temperature operation via residual polar solvents, these highly reactive solvents inevitably trigger severe interfacial parasitic reactions and detrimental polymer dehydrofluorination. To resolve this critical dilemma, we propose a “weak‐solvation reconstruction” strategy by formulating PVDF‐based SPEs with sterically hindered triethyl phosphate (TSPE). By improving ion transport and promoting the formation of inorganic interphases, this weak‐solvation strategy effectively suppresses solvent‐induced corrosion and polymer dehydrofluorination. The customized electrolyte delivers a high room‐temperature ionic conductivity (7.22 × 10−4 S cm−1) and a K+ transference number of 0.58. Symmetric K|TSPE|K cells achieve stable plating/stripping exceeding 5500 h. Furthermore, K|TSPE|PB batteries demonstrate 82.8% capacity retention over 600 cycles at room temperature and 90% retention after 180 cycles at −5°C, charting a viable trajectory for safe, long‐life SSPIBs.

title: Structural and Electronic Engineering of Molybdenum Nitrides for Hydrogen Evolution Electrocatalysis
content:
This review summarizes advanced morphological and electronic engineering strategies for boosting electrocatalytic performance of molybdenum nitride‐based catalysts for hydrogen evolution. It also highlights remaining commercialization bottlenecks and proposes four future research priorities: scalable industrial synthesis, advanced operando mechanism exploration, artificial intelligence‐assisted activity optimization, and the integration of molybdenum nitrides as multifunctional components in practical composite electrodes, thereby promoting their practical hydrogen economy applications.








ABSTRACT
Molybdenum nitrides (MoNx) have emerged as promising non‐precious‐metal electrocatalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) owing to their metallic conductivity and Pt‐like d‐band characteristics. However, their practical performance can be constrained by aggregation and restacking, which limit active‐site accessibility, as well as overly strong Mo–H interactions and high water‐dissociation barriers that hinder intrinsic catalytic activity. This review provides a comprehensive overview of morphological engineering and electronic‐structure regulation strategies for addressing these limitations. First, we systematically discuss the relationship between phase‐dependent Mo‐N coordination, Mo/N vacancies, surface oxidation/reconstruction, pH‐dependent active‐site chemistry, and HER kinetics. MoNx architectures with dimensionalities ranging from 0 to 3D are then reviewed in terms of active‐site accessibility, reactant transport, and gas‐bubble detachment. For electronic‐structure regulation, metal, non‐metal, and dual‐element doping strategies are evaluated based on their effects on local electronic structures and intermediate adsorption energetics. Heterostructure engineering is further discussed, emphasizing the roles of built‐in electric fields, bicomponent synergistic effects, and lattice mismatch‐induced defects. These analyses highlight the coupled effects of morphology, electronic structure, and surface evolution in determining HER performance. Finally, remaining challenges and future research directions are proposed for developing robust, scalable, and practically viable MoNx‐based HER electrocatalysts.

title: Exploring the distributional implications of targeted residential electrification in California
content:
Nature Energy, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41560-026-02155-x

Using data from 21,609 homes in California, this study finds that electrification economics vary widely, with homes that have air conditioning better positioned to benefit. Targeted incentives and rate reform could support equitable adoption.

content:

content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79493-7

The SMC5/6 complex protects genome stability, but how it shapes 3D genome folding is unclear. Here, the authors show that SMC5/6 loss in human cells alters chromatin compartments and activates inflammatory and cancer-related genes, changes that are uncoupled from DNA damage.

content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79650-y

Twist-photonics can tailor light-matter interactions but is difficult to integrate into active devices. Here, the authors show a twist-stacked plasmonic metasurface-black phosphorus platform for arbitrary polarization detection, full-Stokes sensing, and polarization-programmable in-sensor computing.

content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79467-9

Designing actuators for artificial muscles is promising for soft robotics, though it is challenging to integrate feedback without compromising performance. Here the authors design thermally drawn hyperelastic fibers that integrate optical sensing and hydraulic actuation for artificial muscles

title: Disturbance increases soil microbiome functional redundancy but decreases capacity for insurance via winnowed environmental responsiveness
content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79487-5

More redundancy doesn’t always mean more resilience. Here, the authors use seven-year-long metagenomics data from soils above Centralia’s coal seam fire to show that heat disturbance increases microbial functional redundancy but narrows environmental responsiveness, potentially lowering insurance against future stress.

content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79342-7

Li and colleagues introduce an mRNA lipid nanoparticle platform for the selective transfection of endogenous T cells within the spleen; by dual-targeted CAR T cell in vivo programming, the authors show that VEGFR2 CAR-T cells disrupt the tumor vasculature, favoring the infiltration and activity of tumor-directed CAR-T cells.

title: Precise regulation of iridium electronic state reversely stabilizes cobalt oxide for practical proton-exchange membrane electrolysis
content: Reducing iridium use without sacrificing activity and durability is a key challenge for proton-exchange membrane water electrolysis. This work shows that confining low-valent Ir within the Co3O4 lattice can electronically stabilize neighboring Co sites, suppressing support degradation and Ir loss. By linking Ir electronic state to catalyst stability, this study offers a general strategy for designing low-Ir, durable anodes for practical green hydrogen production.
journal: Joule

title: Preorganized electrolyte reduction chemistry enables lithium-ion batteries under extreme conditions
content: The reduction propensity of the electrolyte governs the interfacial stability of batteries. By examining solvation participation and electron-acquisition propensity, this work establishes a preorganized interphasial reduction principle that quantifies molecular reduction propensity. Leveraging this principle, we screened 72 molecules and identified CMDO as the effective additive capable of suppressing the side reactions of ethyl acetate at the interface.
journal: Joule

title: Ionic and bicontinuous mesoporous carbon nitride with multilevel structures for continuous tandem photosynthesis of value-added chemicals
content: An amphiphilic ionic bicontinuous mesoporous carbon nitride enables simultaneous photocatalytic co-production of H2O2 and tandem C–H activation/C–N cyclization at the oil-water interface. By repurposing a sacrificial agent into a high-value pharmaceutical intermediate (BzlM), this dual-functional catalyst sustains co-production in a continuous-flow reactor for over 200 hours, offering a generalizable strategy for sustainable biphasic chemical synthesis.

title:
Resolving Ultrafast
Electronic and Chiral Structural
Dynamics That Govern Circularly Polarized Luminescence from Eu(III)
Antenna Complexes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) from chiral molecules and materials has promising applications in display technology, optical sensing, and quantum information science. However, luminescent-state configurations that approach the maximum degree of circular polarization in emission have only been achieved in exceptional cases, most notably in Eu(III) antenna complexes. An open challenge is the understanding and suppression of detrimental relaxation dynamics of the CPL-active state, which can distort carefully designed ground-state configurations and quench luminescence. We now resolve these processes for the prototypical Eu(III) antenna complex CsEu((+,−)-hfbc)4 (hfbc = 3-heptafluorobutyrylcamphorate) by mapping its complete electronic and chiral structural evolution with ultrafast circular dichroism spectroscopy. Combined with transient absorption measurements and electronic structure calculations, we unravel the intramolecular energy transfer from the helically arranged antenna ligands to the emissive metal ion, and extract the stereochemical configuration of all involved excited states through their ligand-centered circular dichroism. We find that population transfer proceeds from delocalized singlet excitonic states via a ligand-localized triplet, while a parallel singlet exciton trapping channel unexpectedly quenches luminescence. Remarkably, excitation of the luminescent Eu(III) ion increases the helical twist of the ligand sphere by 2.7 ± 1.3° toward an ideal square-antiprismatic geometry, where the CPL performance is most favorable. The excited 4f-orbitals thus drive non-negligible changes in the primary coordination sphere, challenging common assumptions in 4f coordination chemistry and elucidating the need for ligand antenna rigidification to maximize the CPL performance of Ln(III)-based emitters. This work establishes a general framework to unravel the ultrafast excited-state dynamics governing CPL emission.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Molecular Origins of
Lithium-Ion Transport in the
Anionic Metal–Organic Framework SU-102
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Metal–organic framework (MOF) quasi-solid electrolytes offer chemically tunable environments for ion transport, but the molecular roles of framework coordination and confined solvent remain unclear. We combined solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR) measurements with molecular dynamics simulations to determine the Li+ transport mechanism in propylene carbonate (PC)-filled SU-102. Variable-temperature direct- and cross-polarization 7Li ssNMR reveal two distinct Li+ populations with different local tumbling dynamics. Our simulations identified Zr-associated, linker-associated, and fully PC-solvated Li+ coordination environments. The most strongly stabilizing Li+ site is not necessarily the one that carries transport: Zr-associated sites bind Li+ most strongly but form a discontinuous network along the pore axis, whereas the weaker-binding linker sites form a continuous one. Linker-associated Li+ also shows faster site-persistence decay and the largest trial-weighted displacement, and linker-to-linker hopping is the most frequent classified event, followed by Zr-to-Zr hopping. Chemical color-diffusion nonequilibrium molecular dynamics yielded an ionic conductivity of 1.34 ± 0.48 mS cm–1 along the one-dimensional channels and negligible conductivity perpendicular to them, giving an orientational average of 0.45 ± 0.16 mS cm–1, in close agreement with experiment (0.52 mS cm–1). Together, our results indicate that PC-assisted hopping between linker sites contributes more strongly than vehicular diffusion of fully solvated ions, with confined PC retained in the coordination shell across these transfers. These findings identify the balance between ion–framework stabilization and facile site-to-site exchange as a key design principle for reticular quasi-solid electrolytes.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Atomically Confined
Structural Self-Compensation at
Grain Boundaries in Ba-Based Layered Proton Conductors
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ion transport and interfacial stability in oxide materials are strongly influenced by the electrostatics that develop at grain boundaries. In conventional ABO3-type perovskites, grain boundary resistance is well-explained by space-charge effects, in which a positively charged grain boundary core is compensated by the accumulation of negatively charged acceptor dopants. By contrast, the compensation mechanism in recently developed Ba-based layered perovskites has remained unclear. In this study, by directly resolving the grain boundary atomic structure of this material class, we identify a previously unrecognized, structurally confined charge-compensation mode. Using atomic-resolution imaging, spatially resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy, density functional theory, Poisson–Cahn calculations, and impedance spectroscopy, we show that acceptor-doped BaZrO3 compensates its grain boundary through diffuse dopant segregation, whereas layered Ba2LuAlO5 and Ba5Er2Al2ZrO13, which possess intrinsically oxygen-deficient frameworks, instead form a BaLnO3-δ-type layer (Ln = lanthanide) immediately adjacent to the grain boundary core. Relative to the diffuse space-charge layer in BZY82, this atomically localized compensation confines the compensating charge to a single structural block, thereby lowering the electrostatic barrier and the grain boundary activation energy for proton transport. These findings establish spatially confined structural compensation as a key determinant of grain boundary charge balance in layered perovskites and provide a general design principle for engineering next-generation, high-performance Ba-based protonic electrolytes.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
1,8-Azulenedicarboxylic
Imides: Excited-State Properties
and Catalytic Activity of a Nonalternant π-System
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Imide-functionalized polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) represent an important class of π-conjugated molecules; however, their nonalternant isomers remain largely unexplored. Herein, we report the synthesis and investigation of the structural, photophysical, and excited-state properties of 1,8-azulenedicarboxylic imides as nonalternant isomers of 1,8-naphthalimides. These compounds retain the characteristic photophysics of the azulene framework, including near-infrared (NIR) absorption and anti-Kasha emission, while substitution at the imide nitrogen enables modulation of their excited-state electronic structures. QD-NEVPT2 calculations identified an S2–T1 pair with relatively large SOC and LE-to-CT character, suggesting a plausible ISC pathway associated with the observed singlet-oxygen photosensitization. Consequently, 1,8-azulenedicarboxylic imides function as an effective visible-light photocatalyst for the α-cyanation of secondary and tertiary amines. These findings demonstrate that the present nonalternant molecular design provides a strategy for tuning excited-state properties by modulating locally excited and charge-transfer states in imide chromophores.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Awakening Latent Diradicals
to Enhance Antiferromagnetic
Coupling between Localized Organic Spin Centers
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Connecting persistent radicals through π-conjugated linkers provides a promising route for developing organic magnetic systems. However, the simultaneous realization of localized addressable spins and thermally robust antiferromagnetic (AFM) coupling remains challenging. Conventional approaches based on quinoidal versus aromatic resonance forms impose electronic constraints that limit access to this regime. Here, we introduce a molecular design principle in which the latent open-shell character of selected heterocyclic linkers is activated to significantly strengthen AFM interactions between localized radical centers. First-principles calculations reveal that this enhancement: i) originates from increased linker spin polarization acting synergistically with partial quinoidalization, and ii) is robust across a series of diradicals combining an expandable family of linkers with representative persistent radicals. We identify diradicals displaying pronounced open-shell character with unusually large singlet–triplet energy gaps typically associated with closed-shell systems. Extending this concept to two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks, we further show that our approach translates from discrete molecules to strongly AFM materials.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Directed Attachment
of Catalysts into the Extended
Environments of Soft Photoelectrodes for Hydrogen Evolution
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present a detailed investigation of early stage photoelectrochemical deposition of platinum nanoparticle (Pt-NP) catalysts on semiconducting polymer platforms for the light-assisted hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) using electrochemical, spectroscopic, and microscopy characterization, combined with density functional theory (DFT) modeling. The photoactive junction─formed from a blend of donor (PTB7-Th) and acceptor (P(NDI2OD-T2)) polymers─exhibits HER efficiencies that increase exponentially with Pt-NP loading (ca. 8.0 × 101 to 2.5 × 104 ng/cm2) of highly faceted Pt-NPs. The blended heterojunction demonstrates acceptor enrichment of the near-surface region as the point of Pt deposition via progressive nucleation, at sites which we posit are the near-surface termini of “fast transport pathways” created within the PTB7-Th/P(NDI2OD-T2) blend film. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), for the lowest coverage Pt-NPs, combined with DFT modeling, suggests Pt–S interactions via the bithiophene groups in P(NDI2OD-T2) might dominate at the earliest stages of Pt deposition, while larger DFT-modeled 14- and 38-atom Pt clusters demonstrate Pt–C and Pt–O═C interactions on naphthalene diimide cores. Collectively, our findings suggest that submicron environments in soft photoelectrode materials function as integrated architectures, as expected, where charge creation requires well mixed domains, adjacent to domains optimized for charge transport. Photoelectrochemically deposited metals such as Pt-NPs decorate the most photoelectrochemically active near-surface regions, producing good HER efficiencies. Hierarchical assembly of such photoactive soft materials has the potential to provide a transformative framework for scalable energy conversion that extends beyond hydrogen evolution.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Piezocatalytic Sulfonation
Enables Nongenetic Competition
Therapy for Colorectal Cancer
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Irreversible post-translational modifications provide a potential means to impose persistent changes in protein function, yet their controlled generation inside living cells remains challenging. Here, we develop an ultrasound-responsive potassium sodium niobate–gold (KNN@Au) piezoelectric nanoheterojunction functionalized with hyaluronic acid (KNN@Au-HA) to enable in situ terminal protein sulfonation. Under ultrasound excitation, the dynamic modulation of KNN polarization generates a piezo-potential that facilitates interfacial charge separation and electron transfer, promoting the single-electron reduction of O2 to •O2–. Meanwhile, Au–S coordination positions thiol substrates in close proximity to the catalytic surface, facilitating the subsequent multistep oxidation of cysteine thiols to the terminal −SO3H state. Using this platform, we identify ribosomal protein RPL32 as a functionally relevant sulfonation target and resolve sulfonation at Cys96 by mass spectrometry. This modification disrupts ribosomal proteostasis, induces NRF2 nuclear translocation and stress signaling, and converts colorectal cancer cells into a competitive “loser” state that undergoes neighbor-dependent apoptotic elimination. In HCT116 xenograft-bearing mice, ultrasound-activated KNN@Au-HA suppresses colorectal tumor growth; analysis of patient-derived single-cell transcriptomic data reveals RPL32 upregulation as a hallmark of the malignant “winner” state, establishing a functional match between this competition therapy and colorectal cancer. Together, these findings demonstrate that piezocatalytic protein modification can chemically reprogram cellular competitive fitness without genome editing, providing a proof of concept for nongenetic competition therapy against cancer.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Unified Asymmetric
Approach to Tetracyclic Diterpenoids
via Ring Reconstruction Strategy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tetracyclic diterpenoids exhibit intricate densely fused and bridged polycyclic architectures and diverse biological profiles, yet their collective asymmetric synthesis from a unified precursor remains a formidable challenge due to immense topological barriers between distinct scaffolds. Herein, we report a divergent asymmetric synthesis of the tetracyclic diterpenoid family driven by a “ring reconstruction” strategy. Commencing with a platinum-catalyzed diboration/tandem allylation to establish the initial stereocenters, we assemble a highly oxidized ent-kaurane central hub via an orchestrated sequence featuring hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and Johnson–Claisen rearrangement. Leveraging this platform, we deploy tailored radical and photochemical skeletal editing to overcome inherent topological constraints. This enables the divergent remodeling of the ent-kaurane core into an array of complex architectures, including ent-atisane, ent-beyerane, jungermannenone, and ent-aphidicolane frameworks. This unified strategy provides an efficient route to complex polycyclic natural products and highlights the power of skeletal editing for rapidly expanding chemical space.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
In Situ Polymerized
Main/Side-Chain Bifluorinated
Cross-Linked Polyether Electrolytes for High-Voltage Lithium Metal
Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Polyether electrolytes are compelling candidates for lithium metal batteries owing to their high ionic conductivity and conformal interfacial contact. However, their widespread adoption is impeded by inherent vulnerabilities, including limited oxidative stability against high-voltage cathodes, uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth, and persistent interfacial side reactions. To overcome these challenges, we report an in situ polymerized cross-linked polyether electrolyte engineered with a bifluorinated molecular architecture (PTFMO-BEP), incorporating −CF2– segments in the polymer backbone and −CF3 groups on the side chains. This design significantly enhances the intrinsic oxidative stability, extending the electrochemical window beyond 5.5 V. Concurrently, the electron-withdrawing fluorinated motifs weaken the Li+-polymer coordination, steering an anion-derived decomposition pathway to form a homogeneous, inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). Consequently, the PTFMO-BEP electrolyte enables exceptional cyclability in Li||Li symmetric cells (&gt;800 h) and uniform, dendrite-free lithium deposition. When paired with high-loading LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 (NCM811) cathodes (∼4.4 mAh cm–2) and thin lithium anode (50 μm), the Li||NCM811 full cells achieve outstanding capacity retention of 85.6% after 150 cycles at 4.3 V and 91.5% after 100 cycles at 4.5 V. Remarkably, stable operation is maintained even under an ultrahigh cutoff voltage of 4.7 V with a 20 μm Li anode (88.7% retention over 100 cycles). Furthermore, ampere-hour-scale pouch cells configured with LiNi0.90Co0.05Mn0.05O2 (NCM9055) cathodes deliver a high gravimetric energy density of 510.1 Wh kg–1. This work exemplifies a potent molecular-design strategy to advance polyether electrolytes for practical high-energy-density lithium metal batteries.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Three-Motif-Based
One-Dimensional Covalent Organic
Framework as an Efficient Cathode Material for Stable Rechargeable
Sodium-Ion Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Crystalline one-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (1D COFs) hold great promise for diverse applications; however, their synthesis remains challenging, as it requires simultaneous control over chain dimensionality and crystallization of polymeric chains that are intrinsically prone to entanglement. Here, we show that benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b′]difuran-2,6(3H,7H)-dione (BDFO), in the presence of isoquinoline, effectively compels the trifunctional monomer 2,4,6-tris(4-formylphenyl)-1,3,5-triazine (TPFT) to polymerize as a V-shaped ditopic linker, affording 1D zigzag chains that stack in a staggered arrangement to form the crystalline porous framework (CityU-31). CityU-31 exhibits a rectangular nanowire morphology with well-defined lattice fringes, a narrow pore-size distribution of 1–2 nm, and a surface area of 185 m2 g–1. Importantly, the V-shaped connectivity leaves one formyl group at each TPFT unit unreacted, and these pendant aldehydes serve as built-in handles for postsynthetic functionalization. As a proof of concept, a third motif was covalently linked via Knoevenagel condensation, converting the aldehyde groups into cyano functionalities to yield CityU-31-CN. Endowed with the cyano-decorated 1D backbone, CityU-31-CN delivers an extended voltage window (0.8–3.5 V), a high capacity of 160 mAh g–1 at 0.1 A g–1, and outstanding cycling stability (&gt;10,000 cycles). The intrinsic backbone reactivity of CityU-31 thus offers a versatile platform for postsynthetic modification, greatly expanding the application scope of crystalline 1D polymers.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Enhancing Grignard
Reactions via Anion Borrowing in
Deep Eutectic/Organic Biphasic Media
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rational optimization of the Grignard reaction remains a considerable challenge for synthetic chemists. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as powerful reaction media to enhance nucleophilic additions to unsaturated organic molecules. In this protocol, a solution of the Grignard in THF is added to the DES containing the substrate under vigorous stirring. In this study, we determine the underlying causes for this beneficial effect by combining ab initio molecular dynamics, QM/MM simulations, and enhanced sampling, using i-PrMgCl and acetophenone as reagents, THF as the organic solvent, and a 1:2 solution of choline chloride:glycerol as the DES. Our results demonstrate enhanced chemoselectivity for the Grignard addition over β-H transfer side reaction from the isopropyl group when in DES/THF. This enhanced selectivity stems from the formation of chlorinated dimagnesium entities at the DES interface. While the neutral Grignard species in neat THF kinetically favors β-H transfer, chloride enrichment from the DES renders both pathways kinetically competitive and markedly increases the thermodynamic preference for the addition product through enhanced intramolecular stabilizing interactions. This is in line with experimental evidence of increased selectivity in the presence of various halide salts. This mechanistic interpretation paves the way for the rational improvement of Grignard reagents, allowing an even broader application of these compounds in these nonconventional solvents.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
8-Oxoguanine
Is the Major Product of the Reaction
of Guanine Radical Cations with •NO2:
A Spin-Orchestrated, Anisotropic Reaction Landscape and Its Biological
Implications
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Formation of guanine radical cations (G•+) represents a hallmark DNA lesion produced by ionizing radiation and one-electron oxidation processes. •NO2, a reactive nitrogen species in living systems, drives nitrative and oxidative damage linked to mutagenesis and inflammation. Herein, we delineate spin-orchestrated interactions between •NO2 and radical cations of 2′-deoxyguanosine (dGuo•+) and its model compound 9-methylguanine (9MG•+) to probe synergistic pathways that exacerbate guanine nucleobase and nucleoside damage. Kinetic energy-resolved reaction coupled with mass spectrometric measurements revealed distinct pathways governing regioselective nitrite- and nitro-additions, adduct decomposition, and charge transfer. Direct dynamics simulations and potential energy surface analyses of the 9MG•+ + •NO2 model system, using spin-projected and time-dependent DFT, CCSD(T), and CASPT2 theories, characterized reaction mechanisms, thermodynamics, and kinetics arising from anisotropic interactions within open-shell 1,OS[G•+(↑)···(↓)•NO2] and 3[G•+(↑)···(↑)•NO2]. Through radical combination, the reaction system advances through multiple excited electronic and vibrational manifolds while preserving spin states (no intersystem crossing); only singlet states are open to chemical transformations. •NO2 markedly amplifies the lesion of guanine radicals by promoting sequential electron and H loss, producing 8-oxoguanine in neutral, radical cation, and doubly oxidized forms, along with release of •NO, NO+, and HNO. These pathways proceed through nitrite addition rather than guanine nitration, and HNO forms through •NO-mediated hydrogen abstraction via both conventional and roaming mechanisms. The studies identified new routes to the 8-oxoguanine lesion that has been traditionally attributed to reactive oxygen species. The biological implications of •NO2-mediated damage to guanine radical cations are discussed.</jats:p>

Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Palladium-Catalyzed
Enantioselective Oxidative Remote
(4 + 1)-Cyclization of 1,6-Enynes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed enantioselective oxidative remote (4 + 1) cyclization of 1,6-enynes using PhI(OPiv)2 as the oxidant. Both Z- and E-enynes are competent substrates, affording the same cyclopentane-fused lactones and lactams with high efficiency, and excellent enantioselectivity is achieved using chiral pyridinyl oxazoline ligands. These cyclopentane-fused lactones can be readily transformed to other chiral cyclopentane derivatives. Notably, the use of TFE as the solvent is critical for attaining high chemoselectivity and enantioselectivity. Density functional theory calculations reveal that unlike previous reports of asymmetric enyne cyclization, the enantioselectivity of this reaction is governed by cis-oxypalladation of the alkyne. The resulting vinyl-Pd(II) intermediate undergoes sequential alkene insertion, palladium migration, and oxidation steps. The generated terminal alkyl-Pd(IV) species then undergoes an SN2-type reductive elimination with the enol ester as the nucleophile, which accounts for the formation of the cyclopentane skeleton.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Multiscale Modeling
of Virus Capsid Self-Assembly
Reveals How Small Molecule Antivirals Can Redirect Assembly Pathways
and Products
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Controlling the assembly of a virus capsid, a regular complex of hundreds of subunits, has applications for development of antivirals and for development of nanocontainers. Recent work has shown that a class of small molecules called capsid assembly modulators (CAMs) is promising for treating Hepatitis B virus (HBV). CAMs bind to HBV capsid proteins and alter their self-assembly, leading to nonfunctional and malformed structures. The mechanisms by which CAMs alter capsid assembly remain unclear. Here, we use a kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) model for HBV capsid assembly to simulate how CAMs affect this complex reaction. The model is parametrized from all-atom simulations, resulting in unprecedented correlation between simulation and biochemical and structural observations. Simulations reproduce the effect of CAMs on experimental assembly products and their distributions. By analyzing assembly trajectories, we clarify the roles of thermodynamics and kinetics in determining assembly products, identify assembly mechanisms, and predict the key intermediates that lead to either capsids or malformed structures. Our findings enhance our fundamental understanding of capsid assembly, help advance the development of CAMs as a treatment for HBV and, more broadly, inform efforts to direct self-assembly pathways toward specific products.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Terahertz Stimulation
Enhances Nanopore Capture Rate
via Mitigating Voltage-Induced Water Compression
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanopore sensing has emerged as a powerful tool for proteomic analysis, yet controlling molecular translocation, particularly for neutral residues, remains a significant challenge. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the translocation of electrically neutral peptides and amino acids, and to elucidate how nanoslit geometry and applied voltage jointly regulate the process from both kinetic and thermodynamic perspectives. As the applied voltage increases from 0 to 1 V, the biomolecule capture time doubles, whereas the dwell time is reduced by half. Potential-of-mean-force calculations reveal a higher entry barrier and a lower exit barrier. Further analyses of solvent density and the corresponding bulk-equivalent pressure show that increasing the voltage or narrowing the nanoslit raises the density of the confined solution, generating a bulk-equivalent static-pressure differential that increases resistance to molecular entry while reducing resistance to exit. To relieve this voltage-induced compression, we apply an external terahertz (THz) electromagnetic stimulation, which effectively shortens the capture time by lowering the entry barrier from 48.49 to 38.76 kJ/mol. This study provides molecular-level insights into nanopore translocation and offers practical strategies to enhance molecular capture, potentially advancing nanopore proteomics and informing related applications. Notably, this computational research is the first to introduce THz stimulation for regulating nanopore translocation, offering a noncontact approach to mitigate water compression, as well as for active and reversible nanopore control.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Defect-Mediated On–Off
Growth in Tautomeric
Crystallization: The Curious Case of Theophylline Monohydrate
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Crystal growth is inherently sensitive to interfacial structure, yet it remains poorly understood how intrinsic molecular heterogeneity in tautomeric materials translates into dynamic growth behaviors. Here, we combine microfluidics, in situ atomic force microscopy (AFM), molecular dynamics (MD), and density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the crystallization of theophylline monohydrate, which exhibits a minor tautomer (TP-N9, percent-level) coexisting in growth solutions with the dominant lattice-forming species (TP-N7). Facet-resolved measurements show that the (101̅) and (103̅) surfaces exhibit markedly different growth kinetics owing to their distinct interfacial structures, including transitions between arrested and active growth states. On basal (011) and (01̅1) planes, we observe anisotropic step propagation arising from direction-dependent molecular packing at step edges, which impose conformational constraints on solute incorporation into surface growth sites. Despite its low abundance, the TP-N9 tautomer functions as a growth inhibitor and exerts a disproportionate, facet-dependent influence on surface growth. MD simulations indicate that solute adsorption strength alone cannot explain growth rate anisotropy; instead, adsorption in growth-incompatible configurations appears critical, with growth rates governed by the energetic barriers for post-adsorption rearrangement into registry with the crystal lattice. Time-resolved measurements across a range of synthesis conditions revealed defects that transiently pin advancing steps, persist through partial overgrowth, and create local strain, which we attribute to TP-N9 adsorption. These collective effects give rise to spatially heterogeneous growth and dissolution and, macroscopically, drive defect-mediated on–off growth through dynamic shifts in faceting. These results reveal how trace-level tautomeric heterogeneity can redirect crystal growth through facet-dependent incorporation and defect-mediated kinetic regulation.</jats:p>

title:
Accessing Alkyl Linkers
for Macrocyclic Peptide Synthesis
via Nickel-Mediated Doubly DeAminative Macrocyclization
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rise of macrocyclic peptides as a therapeutic modality has exposed gaps in the synthetic chemistry toolbox available for drug discovery teams to rapidly explore diverse linkers for structural optimization. In contrast to the thioether linkers common in peptide leads identified from mRNA display, all-carbon linkers are desirable for imparting solubility and stability, but existing approaches suffer from limited amino acid diversity, incompatibility with solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), stereochemical loss, multistep requirements, or restricted linker placement. We report a Doubly DeAminative Macrocyclization (D2AM) to install alkyl linkers via C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation. This method uses pyridinium monomers derived from commercial amino acids that are stable to SPPS for the seamless synthesis of complex macrocyclic and polycyclic peptides with conservation of stereochemistry. This deaminative method is anticipated to accelerate optimization of peptide macrocycle structure in drug discovery.</jats:p>

title: In Situ STEM Imaging of Colloidal Crystals Based on Programmable Atom Equivalents
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>It is challenging to image the assembly of colloidal crystals composed of programmable atom equivalents (PAEs) using electron microscopy (EM). PAEs typically consist of nanoparticle cores densely functionalized with radially oriented DNA shells, which assemble in the liquid phase via DNA bonds. EM requires high-vacuum conditions, and electron beams can damage soft materials like nucleic acids. Here, we present a liquid-phase scanning transmission electron microscopy (LPSTEM) method for imaging PAEs composed of ∼5 nm gold nanoparticle cores in solution, enabling the direct investigation of their DNA-directed assembly processes. This system is particularly well-suited for in situ studies of soft-matter dynamics because the gold nanoparticle cores provide strong electron contrast. Using a nanofluidic liquid cell, the nucleation and growth of PAE assemblies, governed via the principles of colloidal crystal engineering with DNA, were directly observed. Imaging conditions were established to resolve colloidal assemblies in liquid while also characterizing electron-beam-induced damage under both conventional STEM and STEM-in-SEM conditions. Quantitative image analysis reveals changes in local coordination during crystal growth and subsequent beam-induced dissociation. Complementary ex situ simulations corroborate that radiolytic species generated in the buffer are major contributors to beam-induced damage. Together, these results establish a versatile and accessible platform for probing the in situ dynamics of PAE assembly in liquids, with broad applicability to the study of other soft nanomaterials and composites relevant to sensing, actuation, energy storage, catalysis, and medicine.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Development
and Application of Nanopore Direct RNA
Sequencing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Individual RNA strands can be sequenced directly using nanoscale protein pores. This process, Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing (Nanopore DRS), uses a helicase motor protein to regulate RNA displacement through the nanopore orifice in single nucleotide steps. Partial blockade of the monovalent ionic current is recorded at 4 kHz and converted to a string of RNA nucleotide basecalls using machine learning models. In this review, we discuss the development of Nanopore DRS from 1996 to the present. This includes performance metrics, evolution of machine learning models, and applications of Nanopore DRS to major RNA classes across kingdoms. Advantages of the technology are highlighted with special emphasis on nucleotide modifications along intact single strands. Shortcomings of the technology are also considered along with possible solutions. We close with forward looking Nanopore DRS applications: Single cell RNA sequencing; remote monitoring of infectious agents; principled understanding of nanopore ionic current patterns using all-atoms simulations; global food security; and clinical applications.</jats:p>
journal: Chemical Reviews

title:
Incorporating
Noncanonical Amino Acids for Protein
Structure Analysis: Site-Directed Spin Labeling CW and Pulsed EPR
Approaches
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Site-directed spin labeling in combination with electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy (SDSL–EPR) has emerged as a powerful and highly adaptable platform probing protein structure and dynamics with residue-level precision. In its classical strategy, a stable paramagnetic label, most commonly a nitroxide radical, but not only, is covalently introduced at a predefined position, typically through an engineered cysteine residue. Continuous-wave (cw) EPR spectroscopy provides sensitivity to protein dynamics across a broad range of time scales (and techniques), from backbone motions (ps-ns) to protein complex assembly and conformational transitions (ms-s) or characterization of protein conformational exchange (μs-ms). Pulsed EPR methodologies, particularly double electron–electron resonance (DEER), provide access to long-range distance distributions in the nanometer regime (ca. 2–8 nm) through the measurement of dipolar interactions between pairs of spin labels. Recent developments in the genetic encoding of noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) have substantially expanded the scope of SDSL–EPR by overcoming the intrinsic limitations associated with cysteine-based labeling. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of ncAA-based spin-labeling strategies for SDSL–EPR, discuss the repertoire of reported spin labels and their synthetic routes, and highlight representative applications in structural investigations of proteins in vitro as well as in cellular environments.</jats:p>
journal: Chemical Reviews

title:
Asymmetric Amyloid
Cross-Seeding Beyond “Like-Seeds-Like”
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Amyloid cross-seeding has often been viewed as a “like-seeds-like” extension of homologous nucleation, in which structurally similar amyloid proteins reciprocally accelerate assembly through a shared cross-β architecture. Increasing evidence instead reveals frequent asymmetry: A→B and B→A can differ in rate, mechanism, structural outcome, and biological consequence, and may change with seed state, fibril polymorph, or microenvironment. Here, we propose that productive cross-seeding is governed by directionally selective compatibility rather than generic β-sheet similarity. We examine six mechanistic origins of asymmetry: conformational selection and population shift, fibril-end templating, dock-and-lock kinetic gating, lateral-face recognition, surface-catalyzed secondary nucleation, and coaggregation coupled to strain selection. We integrate kinetic, structural, cellular, animal, and human evidence, emphasizing that bulk aggregation measurements alone cannot distinguish templated elongation from secondary nucleation, adsorption, sequestration, coaggregation, or strain conversion. We further discuss how heterotypic interfaces reshape fibril polymorphism and disease relevance, and assess emerging molecular-simulation and machine-learning approaches for predicting directional cross-seeding. This mechanism-centered framework provides a basis for understanding mixed amyloid pathologies and for developing strategies to block, redirect, or exploit heterotypic propagation in disease.</jats:p>
journal: Chemical Reviews

title:
Substitution
Reactions of Halogen-Substituted Acetals:
Glycosylations and Related Reactions
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The nucleophilic substitution reactions of halogen-substituted acetals are useful for the synthesis of a variety of compounds, most particularly of sugar derivatives. This review will summarize the current understanding of the mechanisms involved in these reactions and will present substitution reactions of carbohydrate derivatives with fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine substituents. The halogen atom at C-2 can have a powerful influence on the stereoselectivities of the glycosylation reactions, most often leading to 1,2-trans stereoselectivity. Examples of the uses of these halogen-substituted products will also be provided.</jats:p>
journal: Chemical Reviews

title: Reaction‐Induced Dynamic Covalent Networking Enables Adaptive Vesicles and Hierarchical Biointerfaces
content:
Reaction‐induced dynamic covalent networking drives the formation of mechanically reinforced adaptive vesicles that spontaneously assemble into universal bioactive coatings on chemically diverse implant surfaces via a one‐step dip‐coating process. The dynamic covalent interface integrates structural robustness with environmental responsiveness, enabling stable and adaptive interactions across biological and abiotic boundaries. This strategy provides a generalizable route for engineering failure‐resistant multifunctional implant interfaces.








ABSTRACT
Conventional vesicular assemblies often face challenges in balancing mechanical robustness with structural adaptability. Here, we develop a reaction‐induced dynamic covalent networking (RIDCN) strategy that integrates vesicle construction with adaptive biointerface engineering. Through the formation of interconnected imine and boronate ester linkages, RIDCN directs the assembly of non‐amphiphilic building blocks into vesicular structures, with dynamic covalent networks serving as integral membrane frameworks. This structural integration reinforces vesicle mechanics while preserving adaptive reorganization through reversible bond exchange. Beyond individual vesicles, RIDCN enables interfacial assembly on diverse implant substrates, forming adaptive coatings with antibacterial, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and osteogenic activities. These findings demonstrate the potential of RIDCN to connect vesicle construction, mechanical adaptation, and multifunctional biointerface engineering within a unified material design strategy.
