title:
High-Performance
Narrowband Near-Ultraviolet Photodetector
with Array-Based Dynamic Imaging
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Microfluidic technology has become a central platform in life sciences and medical diagnostics due to its unique advantages in manipulating fluids at the microscale. However, traditional fluorescence-based imaging and detection rely on complex optical setups and molecular labeling, which can complicate the development of compact and integrated optical sensing and imaging systems. Here, we propose a narrowband near-ultraviolet photodetector (NB-PD) based on a polycarbazole/carbon nanotubes composite, which intrinsically achieves spectral selectivity through material absorption, enabling narrowband detection without external optical filters. The device exhibits a high responsivity of ∼105 A/W and a high specific detectivity of ∼1015 Jones, demonstrating high photodetection performance among organic and carbon-based photodetectors. Furthermore, a 64 × 64-pixel imaging array is developed to explore static and dynamic imaging capabilities, demonstrated by imaging the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of fluids, as a preliminary demonstration of the imaging functionality of the proposed photodetector. The combination of high spectral selectivity and scalability provides a strategy for integrated, narrowband optoelectronic sensing and imaging, offering a promising approach for future applications in fluidic and biorelated sensing.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
All-Inorganic
Perovskite Nanocrystal Scintillators
with Controllable Ion Migration for Dual-Mode Multienergy X-ray
Imaging
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Multienergy X-ray imaging (MEXI) represents a pioneering technology that surpasses conventional single-energy X-ray imaging, providing more detailed material-specific information for high-precision detection. In this study, we report the synthesis and functional modification of all-inorganic CsPbBrI2 nanocrystals with controllable ion migration, which serve as scintillators for dual-mode X-ray imaging. By exploiting the reversible photo- and thermally induced isomerization of azobenzene-4,4′-dicarboxylic acid (AZ 4,4) molecules and their ion-capturing ability on nanocrystal surfaces, the luminescent peaks of nanocrystals can be dynamically and reversibly tuned within the 600–630 nm range. These tunable photon bandgaps of material are available to transform a range of X-rays into visible spectra-range scintillations for hyperspectral imaging. Notably, this single scintillator material enables either conventional single-energy X-ray imaging or time-correlated multispectral energy imaging after ultraviolet light irradiation. It also demonstrates excellent mechanical flexibility and stability, achieving a remarkable detection limit of 50 nGy s–1 and a spatial resolution of 9 lp mm–1. This work establishes a novel approach for multifunctional X-ray imaging only using all-inorganic perovskite material.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Resistive
Switching in Sb2O3 Molecular Crystal with a
Large On/Off Ratio Enabled by Au Electrodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Memristors based on van der Waals (vdW) inorganic molecular crystals (IMCs) are appealing because of their distinctive material properties. Unlike 3D oxides with strong chemical bonds in all three directions or 2D materials with strong in-plane chemical bonds and weak vdW interactions in the out-of-plane direction, 2D vdW IMCs consist of inorganic molecules interconnected via vdW interactions in all three directions. Understanding resistive switching (RS) conduction mechanisms and the influence of crystalline structures in IMC-based RS devices is imperative for improving their memristive performance. Here, we report nonvolatile resistive switching (NVRS) behavior in 2D α-Sb2O3 IMCs featuring vertical metal–insulator–metal device structures. Structural characterization reveals that polycrystalline α-Sb2O3 thin films can be grown on Au bottom electrodes. Significantly, Sb2O3 RS devices show ultrahigh on/off resistance ratios (&gt;108) with distinct RS. We investigate the conduction mechanisms for the high-resistance state (HRS) and low-resistance state (LRS), where thermionic emission and Fowler–Nordheim tunneling govern the HRS and ohmic conduction dominates the LRS. The switching mechanism is attributed to oxygen-deficient conductive filaments, as evidenced by electrical transport characteristics, micro-Raman spectroscopy, and humidity-dependent conductive atomic force microscopy measurements. The scalable, room-temperature-grown Sb2O3-based RS devices can potentially impact emerging electronic applications.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Hydrolysis-Coordination
Competition Unlocks a Hidden
Solubility Window for Wide-Temperature Aqueous Zinc Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Conventional aqueous electrolyte design prioritizes salts with high reported solubility, yet the role of anion-specific interactions in governing salt dissolution remains unclear. Here, we reveal that zinc trifluoroacetate (Zn(TFA)2) exhibits nonmonotonic dissolution in water, evolving from turbid suspensions to clear solutions and ultimately to crystallization as concentration increases. This behavior originates from a concentration-dependent shift in the hydrolysis-coordination balance, involving changes in water availability and Zn2+-TFA– coordination. Concurrently, TFA–-mediated nanoscale ion-associated aggregates evolve, reflecting the structural reorganization of the electrolyte. Introducing acetonitrile further broadens the clear-solution window by reorganizing the hydrogen-bond network and promoting anion-bridged ionic aggregation. This reorganization reduces bulk-like and interfacial water while increasing TFA– participation in Zn2+ coordination, thereby suppressing parasitic water reactions and promoting the formation of a robust anion-derived organic–inorganic solid electrolyte interphase. Consequently, the Zn(TFA)2-based electrolytes sustain Zn//Zn cycling for over 8200 h at −25 °C and enable Zn//PANI cells with capacity retentions of 94.1% after 7000 cycles at 30 °C and 95.3% after 1800 cycles at −25 °C, together with Zn//I2 cells retaining 81.9% after 40000 cycles at 30 °C and 89.4% after 20000 cycles at −25 °C. These findings identify concentration-dependent speciation and accessible solvation states as key considerations for rational aqueous electrolyte design.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Protein
Corona Selectivity on Carbon Nanotube Biosensors
Is Driven by Surface Coating and Chirality
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Semiconducting single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are versatile near-infrared fluorophores that can be engineered to create sensors for biological research and diagnostic applications. SWCNT properties depend on both surface functionalization and underlying lattice structure, defined by the chiral indices (n,m), enabling the development of wavelength-tunable nanosensors. While the principles of specific SWCNT surface modification with biomacromolecules are well studied, the impact of SWCNT surface chemistry and chirality on protein interactions in complex biological fluids remains underexplored. Here, we investigated the role of SWCNT surface coating and chirality in protein corona formation using mass spectrometry-based proteomics. We systematically compared protein corona formation in human blood plasma across single-stranded DNA (ssDNA)- and PEG-phospholipid-coated SWCNTs, as well as across nanotube chiralities spanning (6,4) to (9,4). Our findings indicate that surface coating identity is the dominant factor governing differential protein adsorption. SWCNTs with high binding stability ssDNA sequences exhibited greater protein-corona selectivity, preferentially enriching apolipoproteins and more internally structured proteins, whereas the PEG-phospholipid coating globally reduced, though did not eliminate, protein adsorption. Trends with increasing SWCNT diameter and chiral angle were generally aligned to each other, both associated with preferential adsorption of larger proteins with lower secondary-structure content, while revealing some distinctive protein-property associations, suggesting (n,m)-dependent interfacial differences. Protein corona formation was further shaped by protein–protein cooperative binding effects in a SWCNT coating-dependent manner. Molecular dynamics simulations provided mechanistic support for the experimental finding that proteins with higher glycine content displayed enhanced binding to (GT)6- compared to (TAT)4-coated SWCNTs through distinct glycine-peptide binding modes. Finally, we observed surface modification-specific fluorescence modulation of SWCNTs upon protein adsorption, impacting functional sensing of dopamine as a model small molecule. These insights provide a framework for the rational design of SWCNT-based sensors for protein-profile recognition in complex biological environments.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Growth of Large-Area
Two-Dimensional All-Inorganic
Layered Halide Perovskite Single Crystals
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ruddlesden–Popper layered halide perovskites have garnered significant attention for high-performance optoelectronic applications, including photodetectors, photovoltaics, light-emitting diodes, lasers, and radiation detectors, because of the strongly confined nature of their excitonic states and the reduced dielectric screening effect resulting from the 2D superlattice structure. While current research has predominantly centered on organic–inorganic hybrid variants, their all-inorganic counterparts are anticipated to exhibit superior optoelectronic performance and enhanced stability. However, the synthesis of high-quality single-crystal thin films and the fundamental understanding of basic optoelectronic properties are lacking so far. Here, large-area high-quality all-inorganic Cs2PbI2Cl2 single-crystal thin films with excellent stability and well-defined phase purity were successfully synthesized via low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LD-CVD) using precrystallized powder precursors. The in-plane and cross-sectional HAADF-STEM images visually demonstrate the periodic crystal structure and layered nature of the resulting single crystal. Temperature-dependent photoluminescence measurements provide a reasonable estimate of a relatively lower apparent thermal activation energy (97 ± 19 meV) compared with 2D layered organic–inorganic hybrid perovskite counterparts, which is rationalized by the suppressed dielectric confinement effects in all-inorganic layered lattice frameworks due to the reduced dielectric mismatch between the all inorganic well and barrier compared to the long-chain organic barrier. Furthermore, the fluorescence lifetime (280 ± 12 ps) is significantly shorter than that of 3D perovskites, which is attributed to the combined contributions of an intrinsically high recombination rate and low-energy cascading carrier-phonon interactions enabled by the soft elastic nature of the layered Cs2PbI2Cl2 lattices. The photodetectors based on Cs2PbI2Cl2 single-crystal thin films exhibit a pronounced response in the ultraviolet regime. Our findings provide a synthetic route to high-quality, phase-pure, large-area two-dimensional all-inorganic halide perovskite single crystals, thereby opening broader avenues for advanced optoelectronic device design.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
DNA Sequence-Programmed
Protein Coronas Determine
Intracellular Fate and Proteostatic Stress of Carbon Nanotubes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) show promise for optical biosensing, imaging, and drug delivery, but turning them into safe, precision nanomedicine tools requires understanding how nanotube surface chemistry dictates recognition and processing by cells. Like other nanomaterials, carbon nanotubes acquire a biomolecular corona on contact with biological fluids, and corona identity is increasingly recognized as central to sensor performance and drug delivery efficacy. However, whether corona identity also governs the intracellular fate of carbon nanotubes remains largely unknown. Here, we show that the single-stranded DNA wrapping of (6,5)-enriched single-walled carbon nanotubes reprograms their protein corona, intracellular trafficking, and macrophage response. By profiling (AT)15, (GT)15, and (CT)15 wrapped SWCNTs, we show that the wrapping sequence programs both the protein corona and the resulting proteostatic stress on macrophages. Photoluminescence imaging and confocal Raman measurements reported that (AT)15 is internalized the most yet leaves the proteome and nanotube structure largely undisturbed, whereas (CT)15, taken up the least, undergoes the most aggressive intracellular degradation and drives the highest oxidative and proteostatic stress. Corona proteomics indicated that all three tested nanotubes form coronas with distinct functional identities that are responsible for divergent intracellular routes. Time-resolved intracellular proteomics combined with functional assays resolved how the host cell reorganizes its biomolecular complexity over time, including oxidative outputs, aside from a sequence-independent core response involving particle engagement, phagosomal sorting, and lysosomal processing. These findings provide mechanistic insight into nanomaterial-cell interactions and the wrapping sequence as a tunable, nucleotide-level design handle for controlling the intracellular fate of carbon nanomaterials, with potential implications for safe and effective nanomedicine platforms.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Screening of Single-Atom
Catalysts for Na2S-Mediated Pre-Sodiation and Interfacial
Rejuvenation in Low
N/P Ratio Sodium Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The pursuit of higher energy and power densities in sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) is constrained by the trade-off between multielectron faradaic reaction kinetics and interfacial stability. Here, we develop a catalyst-mediated presodiation and interfacial rejuvenation strategy to address the low initial Coulombic efficiency of hard carbon (HC) anodes and transition-metal (TM) dissolution from high-voltage polyanionic and layered oxide cathodes in ampere-hour-scale pouch cells. Moving beyond empirical catalyst selection, we establish a rational screening framework for transition-metal single-atom sites based on electronic coupling and geometric compatibility with Na2S. Atomically dispersed Co (SA-Co) emerges as the preferred catalyst, reducing the Na2S decomposition potential to 3.49 V. An SA-Co/Na2S@C functional layer enables precise sodium-inventory compensation and simultaneous interfacial rejuvenation. Unlike conventional blended additives, sulfur-derived polysulfides suppress TM crossover and support high-voltage operation up to 4.5 V, while replenished sodium compensates irreversible HC losses and stabilizes the solid-electrolyte interphase. Coupling an SA-Co/Na2S@C-coated Na3V2(PO4)3 (NVP) cathode (18 mg cm–2) with an HC anode under lean-sodium and lean-electrolyte conditions (N/P ratio = 0.4; E/C ratio = 1.2 g Ah1–) yields a 1.1 Ah pouch cell retaining 97.2% capacity after 200 cycles, with gravimetric and volumetric energy densities of 317 Wh kg–1 and 485 Wh L–1, respectively, and a maximum power density of 831 W kg–1. Compatible with existing electrode manufacturing, this scalable interfacial approach offers a practical pathway toward high-energy, high-power SIBs.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Supramolecular Assembly
Amplifies the Optoelectronic
Performance of Terpyridine-Based Transition Metallomesogens
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>By introducing a supramolecular strategy centered on a novel dendritic ruthenium(II) metallomesogen (Ru-M) functionalized with terpyridine ligands, it is demonstrated that guiding molecular-level hierarchical organization amplifies the electrochromic (EC) performance. Comprehensive structural analyses confirm that Ru-M spontaneously self-assembles into a well-defined and uniaxially oriented lamellar nanostructure. This molecular-level ordering creates highly efficient charge transport pathways, leading to substantially enhanced electrochromic performance compared with the disordered nonmesogenic chromogen (Ru-2Tpy). The organized assembly exhibits remarkable coloration efficiency, a low operating voltage, and superior cycling stability, achieving high optoelectronic efficiency even at a 7-fold lower ruthenium loading per unit area. This strategy of directed supramolecular organization highlights the critical role of nanostructural engineering in overcoming performance trade-offs in electrochromic systems, establishing that tailored supramolecular architectures provide a robust platform for maximizing optoelectronic functionality.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title: Ligand-Mediated Low-Temperature Sublimation Fabrication of Ultrathin-Walled Hollow CuO x Nanocages for Enhanced CO2-to-C2H4 Conversion
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Copper (Cu)-based electrocatalysts are pivotal for driving the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) toward multicarbon (C2+) products, yet their performance is critically limited by the insufficient local concentration and stabilization of *CO intermediates, which severely hinders subsequent C–C coupling. Hollow architectures offer a potential solution via nanoconfinement, yet the synthesis of ultrathin-shell, small-sized hollow structures remains challenging. Herein, we develop a hexadecylamine (HDA)-assisted sublimation strategy that directly converts solid Cu nanoparticles into ultrathin hollow CuOx nanocages at exceptionally low temperatures (≥80 °C). Experimental characterization reveals that oxygen promotes oxidation of the Cu core and formation of a volatile Cu-HDA complex, whose low-temperature sublimation is the key factor for preserving both the small particle dimensions and sub-3 nm shell thickness. Benefiting from the nanoconfinement effect and the ultrathin shells, the as-prepared hollow CuOx catalyst demonstrates outstanding performance in CO2RR. It achieves a C2+ Faradaic efficiency of 52.2%, markedly surpassing the 21.7% of solid Cu counterparts, along with a C2H4 partial current density of 189.1 mA cm–2, which is 8.7 times higher than that of solid Cu nanoparticles. Mechanistic studies further reveal that the highly curved nanoconfinement enriches local *CO concentration, promotes C–C coupling, and effectively suppresses both the hydrogen evolution reaction and C1 product formation. Beyond the specific CuOx system, this HDA-assisted sublimation-driven hollowing approach offers a promising low-temperature route toward the rational design of ultrathin hollow nanostructures with tailored curvature and enhanced mass transport for a wide range of catalytic applications.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Bead-on-Fiber
Nano-Heterostructure Engineering for
Ultra-Wide-Temperature Self-Powered Energy Harvesting and Sensing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) offer a highly promising route for energy harvesting, with the potential to revolutionize multiple fields. However, thermionic emission and material embrittlement at temperature extremes constrain the extension of TENG applications to harsh environments. This work presents a novel bead-on-fiber nanoheterostructure strategy for developing an exceptionally temperature-tolerant and mechanically robust tribo-positive material for TENGs. Controllably growing environmentally resistant charge-lock nanobeads on flexible bacterial cellulose nanofibers delivers structural integrity and stable function to the resulting tribo-layer across a temperature range of −196 to 300 °C. Benefiting from synergistic phonon blocking and pore-size effects, suppressed gas- and solid-phase heat conduction is realized, resulting in an ultralow thermal conductivity of 21 mW·m–1·K–1. This thermal insulation, combined with efficient interfacial charge trapping, enables the TENG to not only retain its triboelectric properties up to 300 °C but also achieve enhanced performance, delivering a high charge density of 115 μC·m–2 at 300 °C. Furthermore, the hydrophobicity and charge-trapping capability of the nanobeads allow the TENG to retain over 95% of its initial output even after liquid-nitrogen immersion. Featuring excellent self-powered intelligent sensing properties under temperature extremes, this bead-on-fiber heterostructure strategy paves the way for ultrawide-range operational systems, enabling extraterrestrial exploration and harsh-environment applications.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Perfluoroalkyl Substances
Detection by Surface-Enhanced
Infrared Absorption Spectroscopy: Two Ways
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Streamlined detection of perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) would greatly facilitate our need to monitor, control, and ultimately diminish human exposure to these environmental contaminants. Here, we demonstrate that surface-enhanced infrared absorption (SEIRA) spectroscopy can offer a practical path to PFAS detection and identification. Both colloidal Au nanoshell-based SEIRA substrates and nanofabricated Au nanoantennas were modified with aromatic amine capture ligands and tested to detect PFAS in water samples. The electrostatic interaction of PFAS with the optimally selected aromatic aminated capture ligands was confirmed using Density Functional Theory. By combining solid-phase extraction, SEIRA, and partial least-squares data analysis, a detection limit for perfluorooctanoate in water of 3.6 ppt was achieved. These findings demonstrate the use of SEIRA as a straightforward, practical, and ultimately low-cost approach for the detection of PFAS in water at relevant concentration levels.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Organ-Specific
Wearable Sensing Systems for Continuous
Plant Health Monitoring
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ensuring plant health has become increasingly vital for sustaining global food security and preserving ecosystem stability. Emerging wearable plant sensing technologies, empowered by advances in functional nanomaterial discovery and nanoscale device engineering, offer a promising approach for continuous and in situ monitoring of plant physiological activities and microenvironmental dynamics. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in wearable plant sensors, organized by their integration with specific organs, including leaves, stems, fruits, roots, and other functional organs. Given the functional diversity and signal specificity of different plant organs, organ-specific monitoring enables a more precise and representative assessment of physiological status. This work summarizes up-to-date wearable sensor types, sensing mechanisms, nanostructured functional materials, device architectures, and highlights representative applications across diverse species. This review provides a framework for designing organ-oriented sensing systems to advance sustainable agriculture.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Single-Crystal-Like
Giant-Grain Oxide Semiconductors
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Controlling grain size in crystalline oxide semiconductors (COSs) has long been a fundamental challenge, with lateral grain dimensions typically limited to several hundred nanometers. Here, we report nucleation-suppression-driven grain engineering in quaternary Al-incorporated In–Ga–O (AIGO) to obtain giant-grain oxide semiconductors (GOS). GOS exhibits giant grains of approximately 18 μm with locally single-crystal-like domains, substantially exceeding the TFT channel dimensions (5 × 5 μm) while being realized through a back-end-of-line (BEOL)-compatible process below 400 °C. Back-channel-etched (BCE) TFTs based on GOS exhibit enhanced electrical performance, with the field-effect mobility increasing from 32.06 cm2 V–1 s–1 in conventional crystalline IGO TFTs to 41.08 cm2 V–1 s–1. More importantly, giant-grain engineering markedly improves device reliability, reducing the threshold-voltage shift (ΔVTH) from 7.21 to 1.38 V under positive bias temperature stress (PBTS), from 8.79 to 0.95 V under negative bias illumination stress (NBIS), and from 10.21 to 1.51 V under negative bias temperature illumination stress (NBTIS). In contrast, excessive Al incorporation suppresses crystallization, resulting in an amorphous phase and degraded device characteristics, highlighting the critical role of composition in balancing crystallization and carrier transport. These findings demonstrate the potential of giant-grain engineering for highly reliable, BEOL-compatible oxide electronics.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Efficient Membrane
Separation of Rare Earth Ions in
Engineered Macrocycle Channels
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Rare earth elements (REEs) are critical components in advanced technologies and are notoriously difficult to separate due to their similar chemical properties. This study explored the design and application of a series of synthetic macrocycles to achieve selective lanthanide separation in a macroscopic biomimetic membrane. We synthesized a set of macrocycles that can integrate into lipid bilayers and demonstrate distinct variations in ion permeability attributed to differences in structural flexibility and specific functional groups. Notably, one of the macrocycles exhibits an 18-fold difference in permeability between neodymium and dysprosium ions, underscoring its potential for selective REE separation. This selectivity was further translated into macroscopic separations in a scalable droplet emulsion-based membrane that achieved a 22-fold enrichment of dysprosium over neodymium from a multicomponent lanthanide mixture under an applied electric field. This work advances the understanding of macrocyclic ligand design, highlighting the balance between molecular rigidity, conformational freedom, and chemical functionalization as key factors in enhancing the selective transport of REEs.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Surface Termination
Controls Symmetric Block Copolymer
Transport through Nanopores
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Understanding how polymer architecture governs transport through nanopores is essential for nanocomposite fabrication, membrane design, and functional coatings. However, the effect of the nanoscale structure of copolymers on chain transport through nanoporous media remains poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that simply inverting the surface orientation of lamellar poly(styrene-block-2-vinylpyridine) (PS-b-P2VP) diblock copolymers, composed of two monomers with strongly contrasting affinities for SiO2, at the entrance of a nanoporous packing of SiO2 nanoparticles significantly alters the kinetics of capillary rise infiltration (CaRI). Using in situ spectroscopic ellipsometry, we find that infiltration of the PS-b-P2VP symmetric diblock copolymer into SiO2 nanoparticle (NP) packings is significantly faster when the P2VP domain is the top layer of the block copolymer film and is therefore the first to contact the NPs, compared to when the PS domain is the top layer. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations reveal that this difference originates from block-specific adsorption pathways that reorganize the nanophase structure around NPs: P2VP-first infiltration forms thin adsorbed layers that drive PS into the pore interiors, producing larger PS-rich regions with greater apparent connectivity, which is associated with a higher upward chain flux. In contrast, PS-first infiltration produces thicker P2VP layers that result in smaller, more fragmented PS-rich regions and a lower upward chain flux. Above the order–disorder transition (ODT), or upon silanizing NPs to neutralize surface affinity, the rate difference disappears. These findings demonstrate how the interplay between nanoscale domain configuration and polymer–surface affinity governs infiltration dynamics, providing mechanistic insight into controlling transport in nanostructured block copolymers and into designing high-loading composites, selective membranes, and functional coatings with controlled transport pathways.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Collective Plasmon
Resonances in Hierarchically Doped
Metal-Oxide Nanocrystal Metasurfaces
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Plasmonic nanocrystal (NC) assemblies produce collective plasmon resonances (CPRs), amplifying light–matter interactions beyond the single-NC limit. Structural and compositional disorder in self-assembled NCs effectively diversify optical responses via inhomogeneous near fields, a heterogeneity that provides a degree of versatility that can benefit applications in sensing and photochemistry. How near-field coupling between spectrally detuned plasmonic NCs sculpts emergent CPR modes and far-field responses remains unexplored. Here, we leverage optical and electron spectroscopies to investigate near-field coupling in hierarchically doped assemblies of plasmonic metal oxide NCs. Similarly doped NCs form coherently resonating subsets underlying CPR hybridization, and near-field coupling between dissimilarly doped NCs locally enhances near fields in a way that cannot be explained by the NC mixing ratio alone. Optical simulations predict that individual NCs are polarized not at their native localized surface plasmon resonance frequency but instead at each hybrid-mode frequency, with coupling either enhancing or suppressing extinction depending on the neighboring NC environment. We experimentally observe this local optical heterogeneity using synchrotron infrared nanospectroscopy, and visualize the coupling-modified near fields by spatially resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy. We further develop a coupled oscillator model that analytically describes CPR hybridization and quantifies how the degree of CPR hybridization redistributes the dipole response of each NC species, an approach that could be generalized to other compositions, such as mixed metallic nanoparticle assemblies. These findings reveal how near-field coupling in heterogeneous NC assemblies governs the emergence of the ensemble response from local to macroscopic scales, providing a conceptual framework for tailored plasmonic metamaterials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Immune and Stromal
Barriers to Active Nanoparticle
Targeting of Claudin-4 in Tumors
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanoparticles with targeting ligands can act as “magic bullets” to selectively target tumor cells, a concept that has captivated the drug delivery field for decades. Using cell culture, engineered mouse models, and spatial imaging, we studied how cellular interactions influence targeting of claudin-4 (CLDN4), a key ovarian cancer target. We coupled the C-terminal domain of Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin (cCPE), a high-affinity CLDN4 binder, to ∼60 nm dextran iron oxide nanoworms (CLIO NW) via click chemistry. Targeted NWs had nanomolar affinity for CLDN4 and specifically targeted CLDN4+ cells in culture and 3D spheroids. After systemic injection in mice, targeted NWs exhibited a long plasma half-life. In bilateral CLDN4+/CLDN4– xenograft tumors, targeted NWs accumulated more in CLDN4+ tumors but were also taken up by Kupffer cells in the liver and CD45+ immune cells in both tumors. Repeating the study with anti-CLDN4 IgG-decorated NWs, we again observed high in vitro specificity but low in vivo selectivity, as confirmed by optical and magnetic resonance imaging. Spatial proteomic analysis of tumors showed that NWs mainly accumulate in tumor cells, immune cells, and myofibroblasts, with tumor core cells mostly negative for NWs. Cell stress and metabolic profiles remain unchanged after the uptake. Coculture of CLDN4+ tumor cells and macrophages replicated the limited selectivity of targeted NWs in vivo and suggested that complement opsonization contributes to limited selectivity. Overall, stromal and immune uptake hinder CLDN4 targeting. Future efforts should focus on understanding and inhibiting nanoparticle uptake pathways to develop molecularly targeted nanomedicine.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Molecularly Programmed
Piezoelectric Peptide Interfaces
Couple Energy Conversion with Cell Recognition for Neural Regeneration
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrical regulation of tissue regeneration occurs at dynamic biointerfaces, where cells integrate mechanical, biochemical, and electrical cues from their surrounding microenvironment. Engineering biodegradable materials that simultaneously establish bioactive interfaces and convert externally applied mechanical energy into localized bioelectrical signals remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we establish a molecular programming strategy for constructing bioactive piezoelectric biointerfaces through sequence-defined peptide self-assembly. Guided by multiscale molecular simulations, an amphiphilic peptide hierarchically assembles into noncentrosymmetric two-dimensional nanopatches in which electromechanical energy conversion, cell recognition, and intrinsic antioxidant activity emerge cooperatively from a single supramolecular architecture. Upon clinically compatible ultrasound stimulation, the engineered biointerfaces generate physiologically relevant electrical potentials while maintaining radical-scavenging activity without inducing reactive oxygen species. The localized bioelectrical communication due to their desired cell-adhesiveness activates calcium signaling, cytoskeletal reorganization, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immunomodulatory programs, leading to enhanced cell migration in vitro and coordinated axonal regeneration, remyelination, angiogenesis, and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in rats. Generally, a general molecular design principle is established linking peptide sequence, hierarchical assembly, and biointerface function, demonstrating that electromechanical conversion and biological communication can be coprogrammed within biodegradable supramolecular materials for neural regeneration.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Ferrohydrodynamic
Microfluidics for Multiscale Bioparticle
Separation and Phenotyping
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ferrohydrodynamic microfluidics uses magnetic nanoparticles dispersed in ferrofluids to generate magnetic buoyancy forces for continuous manipulation of diamagnetic particles and magnetically labeled cells. These forces enable separation and phenotyping of cells, extracellular vesicles, and other bioparticles across length scales, although downstream molecular and functional compatibility depends on controlling ferrofluid exposure and residual nanoparticles. This Perspective examines the evolution of ferrofluid-based microfluidics from size-based enrichment toward quantitative physical and molecular phenotyping. We assess key technical and translational challenges, including biocompatibility, scalable and reproducible device architectures, nanoparticle depletion, quality control, and clinical translation. We also define application-specific priorities and discuss how engineered ferrofluids, additive manufacturing, machine learning, and molecular readouts could broaden the versatility of these platforms for precision bioanalysis.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Self-Assembled
Naphthalocyanine Molecular Lattices
as a Platform for Tunable Quantum Superlattices
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Compared to van der Waals moiré systems, molecular assembly offers an alternative platform for superlattice engineering via heterointegration. The electronic properties of the self-assembled square-lattice monolayer of metal-free naphthalocyanine (H2Nc), in particular its band dispersion and tunability by metal substrates, remain less explored. Using density functional theory, we compare the electronic structure of a free-standing H2Nc monolayer with that of H2Nc lattices assembled on noble metal substrates. In the free-standing film, we identify nearly flat, molecule-localized states and more dispersive bands, each compactly described by an anisotropic tight-binding Hamiltonian yielding band-resolved hopping anisotropies. We further show theoretically the wide tunability of intersite hopping and Coulomb interaction through the dielectric and screening environment. On Ag(100), orbital hybridization between molecular frontier states and the substrate drives finite spectral weight at the Fermi level and local interfacial polarization, enhancing the effective intermolecular hopping roughly thirty-fold and drastically reducing U/t. Experimentally, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy resolves substantial interfacial charge redistribution and an enhanced bandwidth of the highest occupied molecular orbital, with the substrate coupling stronger on Ag(100) than Au(111), consistent with theory. Although static calculations exhibit an intrinsic C2 hopping anisotropy set by the two central hydrogens, thermal averaging over tautomer configurations at 77 K restores an effectively C4-symmetric dispersion while preserving the bandwidth. These results clarify how metal substrates and gates convert H2Nc from isolated molecules into a tunable 2D lattice, and highlight molecular superlattices as a platform in which effective interaction parameters can be widely engineered.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Spatial-Mechanical-Chemical
Synergy in Inorganic-Shelled
Cavities Enables Stable Li–Mg Alloy Anodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lithium metal batteries promise ultrahigh energy density yet are plagued by catastrophic lithium dendrites and severe volume expansion. Conventionally, rational three-dimensional (3D) host architectures have been developed to mitigate dendrite proliferation and mechanical stress. However, the structural collapse of lithium-hosting frameworks under dynamic plating/stripping conditions remains a critical bottleneck. Herein, we overcome this limitation by designing a Li-Mg alloy framework integrated with LiNO3 (LMLN), which yields in situ-formed cavities encapsulated by inorganic shells of high ionic conductivity that kinetically guide inward lithium deposition and promote uniform nucleation via tailored interfacial chemistry. The resulting spatial-mechanical-chemical coupling, realized by a scalable roller-pressing process, delivers a triadic synergy of spatially confined deposition, mechanically robust architecture, and chemically functional interfaces. Consequently, LMLN-based lithium metal batteries paired with commercial lithium-sulfur electrolytes and LiFePO4 (LFP) cathodes achieve 95.6% capacity retention over 300 cycles. Notably, a 1 Ah pouch cell pairing an 80 μm LMLN anode with a 17.5 mg cm–2 LFP cathode achieves 85.6% retention over 400 cycles at 1 C alongside intrinsic thermal safety under nail penetration. This dual achievement of superior 1 C cycle life and thermal robustness in 1 Ah LFP-Li metal pouch cells underscores its potential for moderate-rate, low-voltage storage applications.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Weakly Exothermic
Intermetallic NiBi Anode Enables
Ultrafine Reconstruction for High-Rate Sodium-Ion Storage
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bismuth (Bi) anodes are attractive for sodium-ion batteries due to their high capacity and inherent self-reconstruction into bicontinuous porous structures during cycling. However, rapid surface diffusion of Bi atoms during desodiation causes severe ligament coarsening, which compromises both rate capability and cycling reversibility. Here, we introduce a weakly exothermic intermetallic NiBi anode with small formation energy to address this challenge. The close electronegativity between Ni and Bi results in a small formation energy and metallic conductivity, which favor efficient electron transport and facilitate the breaking and recombination of Ni–Bi bonds during cycling. Meanwhile, the interatomic bonding between Ni and Bi effectively suppresses Bi diffusion and inhibits ligament coarsening during desodiation, enabling NiBi to evolve into an ultrafine bicontinuous porous network with an average ligament size of only 65.3 nm, about three times finer than that of pure Bi. As a result, the NiBi anode achieves a high initial Coulombic efficiency of 91.09%, a reversible capacity of 304.2 mAh g–1, excellent rate capability, and an outstanding lifespan of 20,000 cycles with 93.1% capacity retention. This work demonstrates that weakly exothermic intermetallic design with small formation energy offers a promising route to regulate reconstruction and suppress coarsening for durable sodium storage.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Nanozyme-Fortified
Probiotics with Antioxidant and
Anti-Infection Properties for Synergistic Living Therapeutics of Infected
Diabetic Wounds
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Living probiotics are receiving considerable attention in serving as biosafe and superb antibacterial agents for infected wound healing. However, the inadequate reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging capacity compromises the therapeutic effect of probiotics for infected diabetic wounds with high oxidative stress. Herein, we develop a nanozyme-fortified probiotic (NFP) orchestrating an excellent antioxidative activity and broad-spectrum antibacterial properties for synergistic living therapeutics of infected diabetic wounds. The Cu-doped zinc metal–organic framework (CDN) is synthesized to provide a bimetallic biomimetic Cu/Zn site and is uniformly anchored on the surface of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG). The resultant NFP exhibits four types of enzyme-like catalytic activities for ROS scavenging and demonstrates an excellent antioxidant capability. The superior intracellular antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of NFP are also perceived, ascribed to the regulation of cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, arachidonic acid metabolism, and signaling by interleukins in the cell. The secretion promotion of antimicrobial short-chain fatty acids is triggered by CDN regulation for the physiological activities of LGG, eliciting the well-balanced antibacterial activity of NFP. As demonstrated by the rat model of infected diabetic wounds, application of NFP significantly eradicates bacterial infection, alleviates inflammation by ROS elimination, and directs polarization to M2 macrophages, thereby accelerating wound closure. This work provides a promising living material-based tactic consisting of microbial therapy and catalytic nanomaterials for treating infected diabetic wounds.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Atomic Bridges Directionally
Assemble Nanoclusters
into Conductive Nanowires for Enhanced CO2 Electroreduction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>One-dimensional (1D) nanowires, owing to their directional charge transport properties, represent an excellent catalytic platform for overcoming electron and proton transport bottlenecks in electrocatalysis. In this work, we directionally assemble discrete Cu6 nanoclusters into Cu6 nanowires (Cu6-NWs) using an atomically designed “atomic bridge”, achieving long-range order at the atomic scale. The resulting Cu6-NWs exhibit an electrical conductivity of 8.2 × 10–4 S·cm–1, which is 8 orders of magnitude higher than that of discrete Cu6 nanoclusters, highlighting the superiority of the wire-like ordered structure in charge transport. In the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), Cu6-NWs achieve a Faraday efficiency (FE) of 64.8% for hydrocarbon products (CH4 and C2H4) at −1.1 V, reversing the hydrogen evolution-dominated catalytic behavior observed for isolated Cu6 nanoclusters. Mechanistic studies reveal that the linear configuration of Cu6-NWs strengthens the coupling between electron and proton transport. Moreover, it modulates the d-band center via active-site migration, thereby tuning the activity and selectivity of CO2RR. The atomic-bridge-directed assembly strategy offers a perspective for designing high-performance catalysts.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
AI-Driven Cross-Scale
Simulation of Lithium Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The evolution of lithium battery performance involves complex coupled processes across multiple scales, ranging from electronic and atomic scales to mesoscopic structures and battery systems. Traditional simulation approaches face significant challenges in accurately predicting realistic battery electrochemical responses because of scale-bridging limitations, high computational costs, and insufficient dynamic feedback mechanisms. In recent years, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have provided opportunities for cross-scale simulations by enabling knowledge transfer and intelligent prediction through learning physical representations from data. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries. The review first discusses AI-enabled simulation approaches spanning the micro- to mesoscale, including machine learning potentials (MLPs), AI-driven kinetic Monte Carlo (AI-kMC), AI-driven phase-field modeling (AI-PFM), and AI-driven coarse-grained molecular dynamics (AI-CGMD). It then summarizes meso- to macroscale methodologies, including surrogate models, reduced-order modeling, and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Furthermore, AI applications in multiscale feature fusion, inverse materials design, and battery design automation (BDA) are discussed together with computational paradigms toward digital twins and intelligent battery research and development. Despite substantial advances, several critical challenges, including limited model generalization and insufficient uncertainty quantification, remain. Integrating foundation models, generative AI, and multiscale physical modeling could enable more accurate and computationally efficient battery simulation frameworks. These advances may accelerate the discovery, optimization, and deployment of next-generation energy-storage technologies.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Bioorthogonal Engineering
of Tumors with Bacterial
Antigens Leverages Innate Immunity for Enhanced Adoptive T Cell Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Substantial efforts in adoptive T-cell therapy have centered on boosting T-cell activity against tumors. However, a crucial yet overlooked factor is that the onset and maintenance of T-cell responses are highly dependent on innate immunity. Here, we developed a strategy of engineering tumors with bacterial antigens via click chemistry to cross-regulate innate-adaptive immunity, thereby enhancing the efficacy of adoptive T-cell therapy in solid tumors. The targeted delivery of bacterial antigens is mediated by azido sugar liposomes (TALP) for introducing azide groups on tumors and dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated bacterial membranes (DBCO-BM) to endow tumor cells with the innate immunogenicity of bacteria. Our study reveals that tumors with exposed bacterial antigens trigger innate immune responses for direct tumor killing and drive T-cell tumor infiltration to launch adaptive immunity. The antitumor functions of adoptive T cells are significantly augmented with the cross-activation of innate-adaptive immunity. This study highlights the potential of innate immunity in addressing the suboptimal response of adoptive T cells in solid tumors.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Marine-Inspired
Small Extracellular Vesicle-Loaded
Wet-Adhesive Hydrogel with Sr2+ Release Enables Immunomodulatory
Cartilage Regeneration via Wnt/β-Catenin Inhibition
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Effective cartilage repair remains challenging because hydrogel-based strategies must coordinate structural support, sustained delivery of regenerative cues, immune microenvironment remodeling, and pathway-directed chondrogenic regulation. Here, we report a marine-inspired multifunctional hydrogel, termed GMPSE, constructed by incorporating polydopamine nanoparticles (PDA-NPs), strontium ions (Sr2+), and bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicle (BMSC-sEV)-enriched preparation into a fish-scale-derived methacrylated gelatin (GelMA). GelMA provides an injectable and photo-cross-linkable matrix for conformal defect filling, PDA-NPs contribute to the adhesive and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-scavenging properties of the formulation, Sr2+ provides sustained ionic stimulation, and BMSC-sEVs serve as cell-free paracrine regulators. GMPSE exhibited a homogeneous porous architecture, favorable injectability, elastic-dominated viscoelastic behavior, lap-shear adhesion on glass substrates, and sustained release of both Sr2+ and BMSC-sEVs. Ex vivo lap-shear testing of porcine cartilage–hydrogel–glass assemblies after 10 min of water immersion yielded a nominal apparent strength of approximately 62.4 kPa for GMPSE. In vitro, GMPSE supported chondrocyte viability, spreading, migration, and three-dimensional survival, reduced intracellular ROS levels, attenuated inflammatory macrophage activation and promoted a repair-associated marker profile, and enhanced BMSC chondrogenic differentiation, as evidenced by increased SOX9, collagen type II, and aggrecan expression. Transcriptomic profiling and pathway-reactivation experiments supported a contribution of canonical Wnt/β-catenin suppression to GMPSE-enhanced chondrogenesis. In an acute osteochondral model, GMPSE promoted defect filling and cartilage-like repair tissue formation, supported subchondral bone repair, and increased CD206-associated staining in the repair region at 12 weeks. Overall, this study presents a marine-derived, wet-adhesive, immunomodulatory, and cell-free bioactive hydrogel platform for minimally invasive cartilage regeneration.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Reactive Oxygen
Species-Responsive Diselenide-Bridged
Silica Nanoparticles Reprogram Ferroptosis for Inflammatory Bowel
Disease Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is driven by persistent epithelial injury and unresolved immune activation, yet effective therapies remain limited by an incomplete understanding of its spatiotemporal pathological mechanisms. Here, single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals a previously unrecognized ferroptotic landscape in intestinal mucosa, characterized by rapid depletion of ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) in epithelial cells followed by delayed exhaustion of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) in macrophages. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we engineered a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive nanoselenium to deliver ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) by a diselenide-bridged silica carrier to achieve spatiotemporal ferroptosis regulation. In response to pathological ROS, our nanoplatform rapidly releases Fer-1 to alleviate epithelial injury and maintain barrier integrity, followed by sustained selenium release to reactivate macrophage GPX4, thereby resolving the inflammatory responses. This sequential ferroptosis intervention effectively disrupts the pathogenic interplay between epithelial damage and inflammatory amplification, leading to a robust recovery of intestinal architecture and immune homeostasis with excellent biocompatibility. Collectively, our work identifies ferroptosis as a mechanistic link between epithelial dysfunction and immune dysregulation and establishes a mechanism-guided nanomedicine paradigm for spatiotemporal regulation of inflammatory bowel disease.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Urchin-Like
Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles Lower
Intraocular Pressure through PARP1 Inhibition
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) drives glaucoma progression, yet durable control is limited by incomplete mechanistic targeting and inefficient anterior-segment drug delivery. Here, we identify poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) hyperactivation as a redox-sensitive control node governing conventional outflow failure. In human trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal tissues, upregulated PARP1, following oxidative stress, enforces nuclear retention of the ataxia telangiectasia mutated–NF-κB essential modulator (ATM–NEMO) complex. This suppresses cytoplasmic protein kinase B–endothelial nitric oxide synthase (AKT–eNOS) signaling and depletes intracellular nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), effectively coupling DNA damage responses to nitric oxide deficiency and metabolic collapse. To reprogram this dual enzymatic–metabolic disturbance, we engineer a geometry-enhanced, pH-gated urchin-like mesoporous nanoplatform (hereafter denoted PUON@NMOF) that enables spatially segregated codelivery of the PARP1 inhibitor niraparib and the NAD+ precursor nicotinamide mononucleotide. The spiny nanoarchitecture enhances corneal adhesion and trans-epithelial transport, while the metal–organic framework (MOF) shell provides switchable release under mildly acidic microenvironments. Topical administration achieves preferential accumulation in outflow tissues, restores NAD+ pools, reactivates AKT–eNOS signaling and produces synergistic IOP reduction across distinct glaucoma models. These findings define the redox–PARP1 axis as a druggable vulnerability and establish materials-enabled dual-pathway correction as a strategy for precision modulation of outflow biomechanics.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Interacting Cosolvents-Regulated
Solvation for Rapid
Quasi-Solid–State Sulfur Reactions in Li–S Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Enabling a quasi-solid-state sulfur reaction (QSSSR) using sparingly solvating electrolytes (SSEs) represents a promising venue for lean-electrolyte and high-energy lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries. However, impeded charge transfer at the sulfur surface owed to weak solvation results in slow solid–solid conversion kinetics. Here we describe an electrolyte using dipole-interacting binary solvents with distinct solvation capability that decouples electrolyte bulk solvation thermodynamics from the Li-polysulfide solvation at the reaction site─the electrode surface. This is achieved by combining moderately solvating tetrahydrofuran (THF) with weakly solvating cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME), wherein the outer solvation shell of dipole-interacting CPME-THF preserves weak solvation for Li-polysulfides, and importantly, a fraction of THF participates in the first solvation shell and encourages solvation of the dynamically generated solvated Li-polysulfide intermediates, promoting a rapid solution-mediated reaction at the surface. Our study shows that the altered interfacial reaction kinetics redirects sulfur speciation toward growth of three-dimensional Li2S and textured β-S8 upon discharge/charge. The Li–S cell delivers a capacity of 5.2 mA h cm–2 with an electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio of 3 μL mg–1, and stable cycling of a 2.44 A h prototype pouch cell is demonstrated. These results highlight a molecular cosolvent design strategy that reconciles bulk dissolution and surface reaction kinetics for rapid QSSSR.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Correlating Spin
and Optical Properties of Quantum
Emitters in hBN
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optically addressable spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are well suited for near-surface quantum sensing. They offer bright, wavelength-tunable single-photon emission with high optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast at room temperature. Here, we synthesize a high density of visible defects in carbon-doped hBN flakes with a high yield (14%) of ODMR-active emitters. We find that the zero-field splitting parameter D is directly correlated with the zero-phonon line of an emitter, while the ODMR contrast shows no such correlation. We further analyze an individual narrowband defect showing 68% ODMR contrast and enhance its photon collection by ∼40% using a solid immersion lens. By advancing both the practical synthesis of the spin complexes and the understanding of their microscopic origin, our results move us toward the deterministic creation of ODMR-active quantum emitters.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Guiding DNA Double-Crossover-Tile
Assembly via Regulating
the Growth Pathway
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Double-crossover (DX) tiles are among the earliest and most well-established DNA tile motifs for constructing programmable nanostructures. Many DX-tile assemblies reliably produce micrometer-scale nanotubes that have been widely employed in subsequent studies and applications. Because DX tiles are anisotropic─both in overall geometry and in the arrangement of their constituent DNA duplexes─the resulting nanotubes share a characteristic structural feature: the nanotube axis runs parallel to the tile’s DNA duplexes, while the circumference is oriented perpendicular to them. This preference is attributed to intrinsic curvature that accumulates as tiles join during growth, greater mechanical flexibility of intertile connections perpendicular to the duplexes, or a combination of both effects. Here, we incorporate a single-stranded loop at various positions on a DX tile to investigate whether steric hindrance from the loop can counterbalance this intrinsic curvature, thereby enabling programmable changes in nanotube morphology. Our study reveals a surprising finding: regardless of loop placement position, the resulting nanotubes adopt a geometry in which the DX tile axis is rotated 90° relative to the nanotube axis, and are substantially wider than canonical DX-tile nanotubes. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) reveal the underlying assembly pathway: loop-modified DX tiles first polymerize into single-chain tile-string intermediates through preferential axial sticky-end binding, which subsequently coil and close into tile circles or short nanotube segments that seed the growth and elongation of wide nanotubes. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations show that loop-modified DX tiles are conformationally more dynamic than canonical DX tiles, which likely suppresses lateral growth perpendicular to the tile axis and drives tile-string formation. This work expands the morphological diversity of DX tile-based DNA nanotubes and establishes a design strategy for directing tile-array growth through control of hierarchical assembly kinetics.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title: A tri-phase fuel electrode enabling low-temperature co-firing of high-performance reversible protonic ceramic cells
content: Reversible protonic ceramic cells (RPCCs) offer significant potential for efficient energy conversion and storage at intermediate temperatures. However, their widespread deployment is limited by the high sintering temperatures needed for electrolyte densification, which can cause Ba volatilization and cell bending, compromising structural integrity, and manufacturing reliability – as well by the electrochemical limitations of conventional Ni-BaZr0.1Ce0.7Y0.1Yb0.1O3−δ (BZCYYb) (6 : 4 wt%) bi-phase cermet fuel electrodes. Here, we report a fundamental departure from the long-dominant bi-phase cermet paradigm by introducing BaCo0.4Fe0.4Zr0.1Y0.1O3−δ (BCFZY) as a third functional phase in the Ni-BZCYYb fuel electrode support layer, resulting in a novel Ni-BZCYYb-BCFZY (6 : 3 : 1 wt%) tri-phase composite fuel electrode. The incorporation of BCFZY, as a multifunctional BZCYYb-substituting phase with superior sinterability compared to BZCYYb, allows for full electrolyte densification at sintering temperatures as low as 1200–1300 °C. This represents a reduction of 150–250 °C compared to conventional methods, achieved without the use of sintering aids in the electrolyte layer. The lowered co-sintering temperature effectively suppresses grain coarsening in all constituent phases, preserving a fine-particle microstructure with enhanced open porosity that is crucial for electrochemical activity. Under reducing fuel electrode conditions, BCFZY undergoes spontaneous in situ Co exsolution, generating uniformly distributed metallic Co nanoparticles. These nanoparticles simultaneously enhance electronic conductivity and catalytic activity for hydrogen oxidation and evolution, functioning as a self-activating multifunctional phase. The 1250 °C sintered tri-phase fuel electrode-supported cells achieve a peak power density of 1.14 W cm−2 in fuel cell mode and a current density of 1.47 A cm−2 at 1.3 V in electrolysis mode at 550 °C. This demonstrates a substantial performance enhancement over conventional Ni-BZCYYb cells, particularly at operating temperatures below 550 °C. Notably, stable operation has been achieved in protonic ceramic cells, with 4 A cm−2 in fuel cell mode and 5 A cm−2 in electrolysis mode. Long-term stability evaluations conducted over 690 hours, which included high-current reversible cycling, thermal cycling, and fuel starvation, confirm robust durability of the cell. These findings establish the Ni-BZCYYb-BCFZY tri-phase architecture as a new paradigm for fuel electrode design, redefining the performance and manufacturability boundaries of RPCCs.

title: Synergistic Salt‐Bridge and Hydrophobic Interaction‐Driven Supramolecular Adhesives Enable Ultrastrong Dry/Underwater Bonding and Broad Harsh‐Condition Adaptability: Polyelectrolyte‐Templated Multi‐Promoting Effects
content:
A general polyelectrolyte‐templated multi‐regulation strategy is proposed to establish a new class of cooperative salt‐bridge and hydrophobic interaction‐driven supramolecular adhesives, which overcomes the long‐standing adhesive‐water conflict and achieves solvent‐free, fast and simultaneous ultrastrong dry/underwater adhesion alongside broad harsh‐environment adaptability.








ABSTRACT
Developing advanced amphibious adhesives that perform well in both dry and underwater environments is critical yet challenging for unlocking diverse underwater applications. Here, we propose a general polyelectrolyte‐templated multi‐regulation strategy to establish a new cooperative salt‐bridge/hydrophobic interaction‐driven supramolecular adhesive that overcomes long‐standing water‐adhesive conflicts and attains rapid yet ultrastrong dry/underwater adhesion with broad harsh‐environment adaptability. By engineering branched‐polycationic electrolytes with dense interaction sites as versatile templates, this strategy exerts multi‐promoting effects of polyelectrolytes on dense salt‐bridge formation, precursor wetting and ultrafast solvent‐free curing, which, in cooperation with flexible hydrophobic moieties, optimizes cohesion/interfacial adhesion, balances flexibility‐rigidity and inhibits water‐erosion and interface hydration within cured network. Thus, the optimized b‐PAE achieves ultrahigh dry and underwater bonding strengths up to 20.9 and 13.2 MPa on safety glass within 10 s—a performance integration rarely reported in previous adhesives. It further demonstrates robust adhesion in harsh underwater conditions (seawater, acidic, alkaline solutions), excellent cryogenic tolerance (−196°C) and versatile utility including oil tank leakage repair and rapid pipeline sealing. Mechanistic studies reveal that the synergy of salt‐bridge and hydrophobic interactions governs amphibious adhesion. This universal approach, applicable to various hydrophobic moieties, paves the way for developing diverse amphibious adhesives to advance underwater technologies.

title: N‐Type Organic Ultraviolet Sensor
content:
An ambient‐operated UVA sensor based on n‐type PBFDO exploits oxygen‐mediated carrier trapping and UVA‐induced detrapping to produce persistent and cumulative conductivity modulation. Chemical dedoping further amplifies the response, while the simple device architecture enables flexible sensors, high‐density arrays, optical information storage, and photoelectrochemical transistor operation.








ABSTRACT
Ultraviolet radiation monitoring is important for health, industrial, and environmental applications. Commercial inorganic UV photodetectors offer high selectivity and stability, yet rely on rigid materials and high‐temperature processing, whereas organic UV photodetectors are solution‐processable and flexible but suffer from instability and complex stacking architectures. In this study, we demonstrate ambient‐operated organic UV sensors based on an n‐type conducting polymer, poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO). We propose that thermal treatment promotes oxygen‐mediated carrier trapping that lowers the carrier concentration, while 365 nm UVA illumination induces carrier release and increases conductivity, yielding a two‐terminal device with a broad irradiance range (0.02–500 mW/cm2), large current changes (65%), well‐defined intensity‐time dependence, and reversible reset via trap reconfiguration. We achieve flexible sensors, high‐density arrays, and optoelectronic information encryption. Increasing the degree of dedoping with stronger oxidants raises the relative current change to as high as 17200% under prolonged irradiation, while retaining a reproducible UVA response. We further present organic photoelectrochemical transistors that couple light signals with electrochemical gating to achieve synapse‐like functions. This strategy offers broad application prospects and a versatile design framework for next‐generation organic optoelectronic systems.

title: Ni‐Embedded Carbon Fibers Enable Synergistic Confinement and Catalytic Conversion of Iodine Species for Zn–I2 Batteries
content:
Carbon macroporous fibers with embedded Ni nanoparticles in carbon nanoboxes (Ni@CNBs‐CMFs) serve as an effective iodine host for Zn–I2 batteries. Their hierarchical porous structure physically confines iodine species, while the Ni sites accelerate the I−/I0/I+ redox kinetics through d–p orbital interactions. This combination of physical entrapment and electrocatalysis mitigates the polyiodide shuttle effect.








ABSTRACT
Due to their affordability, safety and high capacity, aqueous Zn–I2 batteries show great potential for large‐scale energy storage. Nevertheless, the dissolution of I3− intermediates leads to the iodine shuttle effect, which results in irreversible capacity loss and poor cyclability, thus hindering practical deployment. Here, we propose a synergistic strategy combining hierarchical pore confinement with catalytic iodine conversion to suppress the shuttle effect. A self‐standing cathode is synthesized, consisting of Ni nanoparticle‐embedded carbon nanoboxes enclosed within carbon macroporous fibers (Ni@CNBs‐CMFs). The abundant hierarchical porous structure provides physical confinement for iodine species, while Ni nanoparticles serve as active centers to accelerate iodine conversion via d–p orbital interactions. Benefiting from the synergistic enhancement in iodine accommodation and reaction kinetics, the self‐standing Ni@CNBs‐CMFs iodine cathode delivers a cycle life of 16 000 cycles with a capacity of 144.5 mAh g−1 and maintains a Coulombic efficiency of 90.0% after a 168‐h resting period. Moreover, the cathode also achieves a capacity of 382.8 mAh g−1 at a current of 2 A g−1 via the I−/I0/I+ redox pathway.

title: Nonpolar Micro‐Environment‐Induced Solvation Field Engineering Enables 600 Wh Kg−1 High‐Voltage Lithium Metal Pouch Cells
content:
A nonpolar microregion‐induced electrolyte (NME) employs propyl propionate to create the Li+‐centered nonpolar micro‐environment that attenuates dielectric shielding and drives PF6− into the Li+ solvation sheath, yielding a CIP‐dominated structure. This NME forms LiF/LiPO2F2 hybrid interphases, enabling stable cycling of Li metal pouch cells (425 and 604 Wh kg−1) under high‐voltage conditions.








ABSTRACT
Conventional‐carbonate electrolytes cannot simultaneously stabilize lithium metal interfaces and sustain fast ion transport. Existing designs mitigate interfacial degradation but compromise ion transport, low‐temperature fluidity, or salt dissociation. Herein, we propose a solvation field engineering strategy via a nonpolar micro‐environment‐induced electrolyte (NME) that overcomes this trade‐off at conventional salt concentration. Propyl propionate serves as an amphiphilic inducer: its carbonyl oxygen coordinates Li+, while its propyl chain extends outward to create a Li+‐centered nonpolar micro‐environment that engineers the local solvation field by attenuating dielectric shielding and strengthening Li+–PF6− interactions, thereby driving a contact‐ion‐pair‐dominated solvation structure. Fluoroethylene carbonate and 2,2,2‐trifluoroethyl methyl carbonate ensure sufficient salt dissociation and high‐voltage oxidative stability. The resulting electrolyte combines rapid ion transport with a robust LiF/LiPO2F2 interphase, suppressing electrolyte decomposition and enabling uniform Li plating/stripping. Consequently, a 4.2 Ah Li||LiNi0.88Co0.07Mn0.05O2 pouch cell (∼425 Wh kg−1) retains 87.7% capacity after 200 cycles, and a 23.5 Ah Li||LiNi0.95Co0.02Mn0.03O2 pouch cell achieves 604 Wh kg−1. The strategy is further applicable to graphite‐based batteries, enabling a 3.6 Ah Graphite||LiNi0.5Co0.2Mn0.3O2 pouch cell to deliver 81.5% retention after 100 cycles at −20°C. NME offers a novel principle to regulate solvation and interfacial stability for high‐energy batteries.

title: A Route to High‐Temperature Creep Resistant Ultra‐High Molecular Weight Polyethylene
content:
The oriented chains of ultra‐high molecular weight polyethylene lead to exceptional mechanical properties, providing light‐weight solutions for demanding applications. However, because of weak secondary interactions, the oriented chains tend to flow at high loads and temperatures, causing catastrophic failure with time. The addition of branches (1‐decene), and their specific distribution along the chain, circumvents failure of the polymer even above the equilibrium melting temperature of unconstrained polyethylene.








ABSTRACT
High‐performance lightweight polymers for load‐bearing applications at elevated temperatures demand strong creep resistance to ensure long‐term dimensional and mechanical stability. Conventional uniaxial drawn polyethylene tapes and fibers suffer from poor creep resistance owing to intrinsically weak van der Waals intermolecular forces, especially above their α‐relaxation temperature (∼90°C) as chain mobility is enhanced. Here we demonstrate that introducing as little as 0.2 mol% 1‐decene branches into low‐entangled ultra‐high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) profoundly suppresses high‐temperature creep. Solvent‐free solid‐state processing at a draw ratio of 250 yields branched and linear UHMWPE tapes with a specific tensile strength of 4.5 N/tex and a specific modulus of ∼200 N/tex. For the constant load of 250 MPa (∼2500 kg/cm2), the linear UHMWPE tape at 110°C accumulates a creep strain of 15%, whereas the branched UHMWPE tapes maintain a negligible creep strain even at 150°C. This exceptional creep resistance is attributed to the ability of the branches to suppress the entropy‐driven relaxation of the oriented chains under constraints. This work resolves the long‐standing high‐temperature creep bottleneck of high‐performance PE, enabling high‐value, sustainable applications in automotive, energy distribution/storage, and advanced structural applications.

title: Electronic Polarization in Covalent Organic Frameworks With Alternating Hetero‐Linkages for High‐Performance H2O2 Photosynthesis
content:
Alternating hetero‐linkage engineering of electron‐withdrawing C═N and electron‐donating C─N bonds in covalent organic frameworks (COFs) induces strong intramolecular electronic polarization and promotes efficient charge separation. The optimal TPPZ‐BC achieves an ultrahigh H2O2 photosynthesis rate of 11.06 mmol g−1 h−1 in pure water under visible light, establishing a strategy for high‐performance COF photocatalyst.








ABSTRACT
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) hold considerable promise for photocatalytic H2O2 production, yet achieving efficient carrier separation and transport to achieve excellent performance remains a significantly challenge. Herein, we constructed a library of polarized COFs featuring alternating hetero‐linkage C═N and C─N linkages, which establish continuous local charge gradients at molecular level. Remarkably, driven by the localized electronic polarization microenvironment, the optimal material (TPPZ‐BC) showed a photocatalytic H2O2 production rate as high as 11.06 mmol g−1 h−1, outperforming most reported COF‐based photocatalysts. Mechanistic studies revealed that the spatial alternation of electron‐withdrawing C═N and electron‐donating C─N linkages induced a strong intramolecular charge polarization. This effect significantly modulates the surface electrostatic potential distribution, increasing the proportion of highly positive regions and thereby enhancing the adsorption and activation of oxygen molecules. Moreover, this structural design breaks molecular symmetry and promotes the synergistic alignment of local dipoles, generating a robust intrinsic electric field. This work provides a new strategy for the development of crystalline porous photocatalysts toward highly efficient photosynthesis.

title: Strain‐Inversion Strategy Enables MOCVD Growth of 53 µm Ultra‐Thick, Stress‐Free, Buffer‐Free III‐Nitride Heteroepitaxial Films
content:
Heterogeneous integration is pivotal for advanced semiconductors, yet residual stress remains a bottleneck. Here we propose a strain‐inversion strategy that transfers misfit stress into the substrate. MOCVD‐grown 53 µm ultra‐thick, stress‐free, and buffer‐free heteroepitaxial GaN exhibits XRC FWHM values of 83/119 arcsec and a TDD of 5 × 107 cm−2, setting a thickness record and enabling high‐performance devices and low‐cost strain‐free substrates.








ABSTRACT
As the semiconductor industry increasingly pivots toward “More than Moore” and “More Moore” paradigms, heterogeneous integration has emerged as a pivotal strategy for achieving system‐level performance breakthroughs. However, residual stress inherent to the integration of dissimilar materials represents a critical bottleneck, directly threatening the integrity and reliability of these advanced systems. Heteroepitaxy, as a representative example, is inherently constrained by stress accumulation, which limits epilayer thickness, increases threading dislocation density (TDD), and degrades device reliability. Here, we present a strain‐inversion strategy that effectively transfers misfit‐induced stress from the epilayer into the substrate stack. Through co‐designed theoretical modeling and experimental validation, we introduce 4H‐SiC/SiO2/polycrystalline‐ceramic‐AlN integrated substrates, and demonstrate metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) growth of 53‐µm‐thick, stress‐free heteroepitaxial GaN films. The films exhibit outstanding structural quality, with full‐width‐at‐half‐maximum (FWHM) values of x‐ray rocking curve of 83 and 119 arcsec for the (002) and (102) planes, respectively, and a TDD of 5 × 107 cm−2. These results not only set a new thickness record for MOCVD‐grown heteroepitaxial GaN but also achieve crystal quality comparable to state‐of‐the‐art benchmarks. Our approach establishes strain‐inverted epitaxy as a highly promising platform for high‐performance nitride devices and paves the way for producing low‐cost and strain‐free GaN and AlN substrates.

title: An Ultrarobust Dual‐Modal Neural Fiber With In‐Sensor Computing (Adv. Mater. 65/2026)
content:
Smart Textile
The cover shows a person touching a garment sleeve with luminous fibers visualizing tactile signals. The in‐sensor‐computing dual‐modal (ID) neural fiber simultaneously senses pressure and position, fusing these features within the sensor while retaining flexibility, mechanical robustness, and seamless textile integration. Tapping and sliding gestures control music players and smart‐home devices, transforming ordinary clothing into an intuitive human–machine interface. More details can be found in the Research Article by Xinqin Liao and co‐workers (DOI: 10.1002/adma.75412).

title: Repairability and Active Defect Utilization in Direct Regeneration of Lithium‐Ion Battery Cathodes
content:
A unified repairability framework bridges cathode failure mechanisms with optimal regeneration strategies. Lithium vacancies, cation disorder, and surface rock salt layers are harnessed as functional resources rather than passive damage. This paradigm shift enables precision routes from relithiation and structural reconstruction to single‐crystal upcycling, offering exercisable guidelines for sustainable closed‐loop battery recycling.








ABSTRACT
Direct regeneration of spent lithium‐ion battery (LIB) cathodes has emerged as a promising route toward closed‐loop battery recycling. Yet most current approaches are fundamentally based on passive defect repair, focusing on restoring degraded materials to their original state. This review argues that degradation‐induced defects should not be viewed solely as damage elimination, but also as structural resources that can be actively exploited to facilitate regeneration and enable materials upgrading. To support this perspective, the concept of repairability is introduced as a descriptor linking failure mechanisms with regeneration feasibility and strategy selection. Multiscale cathode degradation processes are analyzed from the standpoint of repairability, revealing distinct kinetic barriers and regeneration potentials among different chemistries. Regeneration strategies are subsequently reclassified into relithiation, structural restoration, and surface reconstruction, and interpreted within a barrier‐engineering framework where the dominant degradation barrier dictates the optimal regeneration pathway. Beyond conventional restoration, emerging approaches that integrate regeneration with structural enhancement—including defect‐mediated heteroepitaxy, single‐crystal reconstruction, and bulk doping—are highlighted as routes toward cathodes that outperform their pristine counterparts. By shifting the defect repair to defect utilization, this review provides a new framework for understanding, designing, and advancing direct regeneration technologies, ultimately supporting the transition toward a sustainable battery economy.
